pub.passage:
ALTON original passage
The Widow's Ledger

¶1 On a Tuesday evening in March, the Halverton City Council spent forty minutes debating whether a schoolteacher named Priya Castellanos could keep two hives on the roof of her garage. I sat in the back row with a folder of photocopies from the municipal archive, where I have worked for eleven years, and listened to a councilman warn that bees "do not belong in a modern city." He said it as if the matter were settled, as if modern and bee were words that had never shared a sentence. They have shared a great many, and most of them were written in Halverton.

¶2 The first beekeeper in our records was not a farmer but a tanner's widow, Agnes Durrow, who in 1891 set four straw skeps against the brick wall behind her rowhouse on Cordage Street. Her ledger survives, and it is a modest, stubborn document: so many pounds of honey sold to the druggist, so many to the bakery, a jar given to the priest, a sting noted and then forgotten. By 1905 the city directory listed nineteen households that kept bees, and the honey they produced was dark and faintly mineral, flavored by the linden trees the city had planted along the trolley lines. The bees, in other words, did not merely tolerate the city; they ate it, and gave something back.

¶3 Then came 1923. A boy on Fulling Lane was stung several times after poking a hive with a broom handle, and the Halverton Evening Courier ran the story under a headline that called the bees "a swarm of menace." Within a month the council passed an ordinance forbidding hives within the city limits, and within a year the nineteen households had become none. Nothing had changed about the bees. What had changed was the story the city told about itself: it was becoming a place of paved streets and electric signs, and a straw skep behind a rowhouse looked, suddenly, like a thing left over from a slower century. The ban was less a response to danger than a tidying away of the past.

¶4 I do not want to pretend the worries were all invented. Bees sting, and a hive placed on a fire escape above a crowded sidewalk is a poor neighbor; the boy on Fulling Lane spent two days in bed, and his mother's anger was neither foolish nor small. But a city that outlawed every creature capable of causing two days in bed would have to begin with its horses, its trolleys, and its own citizens. The question was never whether bees could do harm. The question was whether the harm was large enough to justify erasing a practice that fed bakeries, pollinated gardens, and gave a tanner's widow a trade of her own.

¶5 The practice did not stay erased. In 1974 a retired machinist named Oscar Lindqvist quietly installed a hive on the roof of a shuttered hat factory, and the inspectors who discovered it three summers later could not bring themselves to write him up. The ordinance was repealed in 1981, and the hives came back the way weeds come back to a vacant lot, first in one place, then in a dozen, then everywhere the sun reached. Today the archive holds photographs of hives on the library roof, in the courtyard of the firehouse, and behind the same rowhouse on Cordage Street where Agnes Durrow kept hers.

¶6 So when the councilman says bees do not belong in a modern city, I want to hand him the ledger. Bees have belonged to Halverton for longer than its sewers, its streetlights, or its council chamber. What they ask of us is small: a roof, a water dish, a measure of patience with the occasional sting. What they offer in return is a reminder that a city is not only pavement and ordinance but a living thing, and that the people who tend small, stubborn, useful work in its corners are not relics of a slower century. They are the ones who keep it alive.

pub.passage:
ALTON original passage
What the Rock Teaches

¶1 On the first morning of the Keeper's School, the fog at Harrow Point was so thick that the eleven-year-olds could not see the lantern room from the landing, and one of them asked, reasonably, whether the lighthouse was still there. We climbed the hundred and twelve iron steps anyway. At the top, a girl named Pilar pressed her palm against the cold glass and announced that she could hear the shoal breaking even though she could not see it, and for the next ten minutes the whole class stood silent, listening to a hazard they had only ever read about. No worksheet I have ever written produced that silence.

¶2 I raise this scene because the Trust's board, at its spring meeting, asked a fair question: is a program that requires a ferry, a tide window, and a volunteer with a first-aid certificate really worth running when the same lessons could be taught in a heated room on the mainland? My answer, after one full year and fourteen visiting classes, is that the same lessons cannot be taught there, because at Harrow Point the building itself does most of the teaching. A lighthouse is not a backdrop for a curriculum; it is the curriculum.

¶3 Consider what the place demands before anyone opens a notebook. To arrive at all, students must read a tide table, because the landing floods two hours either side of high water. To climb, they must count their own breaths on the stairs and notice that the air grows colder as they rise. To understand why the lamp was built where it was, they must stand in the lantern room and look at the charted line of Castell Shoal, then look at the actual water and find the pale seam where the swell stumbles over rock. Every one of these tasks is a lesson in observation, and not one of them was designed by me. The keepers who logged the weather here for ninety years were, without knowing it, writing a textbook, and the children who copy their entries into fresh logbooks are not studying history so much as joining it.

¶4 I will not pretend the arrangement is convenient. The ferry costs the Trust roughly 340 dollars per crossing, three classes this year were cancelled by weather, and at least one student in every group is quietly, miserably seasick before we reach the dock. A thoughtful colleague on the mainland put the objection to me plainly: a good teacher can make a parking lot into a laboratory, so why spend the money on a rock? She is right that a good teacher can do a great deal. But the parking lot does not flood on schedule, does not rise a hundred feet into the wind, and does not keep a ninety-year record of its own weather. The teacher supplies the questions; the lighthouse supplies the consequences.

¶5 The consequences are what students remember. Of the 312 children who visited this year, 71 returned a follow-up postcard, and the ones we received did not mention the Fresnel lens or the vocabulary list. They mentioned the stairs, the fog, the moment the horn sounded, and the entry they wrote in the log. A boy from Saltmarsh Reach wrote that he now checks the tide before his family goes crabbing, which is, when you think about it, exactly what the lighthouse was built to make people do.

¶6 So I am asking the board to keep the ferry running, and I am asking members reading this column to say so at the autumn meeting. Harrow Point was decommissioned in 1994 because ships no longer needed it to find the shoal. It turns out that children still do.

pub.passage:
ALTON original passage
Standing on Her Work

¶1 One Tuesday last October, a date-formatting library called tidyclock vanished from the public package registry, and by morning several thousand websites could no longer tell their users what day it was. Its sole maintainer, a retired schoolteacher in Pell Harbor, had deleted it after a decade of unpaid work and one rude bug report too many. Desmond Alcock's new book, Nobody's Job, opens with that night, and it is the right place to begin. I spent nine years maintaining a small text-parsing library used by companies I was never allowed to name, so I read Alcock with the uneasy attention of a patient reading her own chart.

¶2 The book's first half is a diagnosis, and it is a good one. Alcock surveyed four hundred of the most heavily downloaded packages in three programming languages and found that more than half depended on a single active volunteer. He calls these projects load-bearing walls that no inspector has visited, and the metaphor earns its keep: the walls are hidden inside the plaster of every bank, hospital, and school district that runs code on top of them. Nobody chose this arrangement. It accreted, one convenient download at a time, until the whole structure rested on the patience of people who could stop at any moment and owed us nothing if they did.

¶3 It is in the second half, where Alcock turns from diagnosis to cure, that the book loses its footing. His remedy is sponsorship: corporations that profit from open-source software should fund its maintainers, and he describes several foundations that already do so. I will grant that money has saved projects. A stipend kept at least one widely used encryption library alive after its maintainer nearly quit, and Alcock tells that story well. But a stipend changes what the work is. Consider the neighbor who shovels the shared walkway every winter because no one else will; the day you start paying her, the shoveling becomes a service, the snow becomes her problem, and you acquire the right to complain about ice. Sponsorship converts a gift into a contract, and the contract arrives written in the sponsor's priorities, not the project's.

¶4 I know something about how such gifts are received. In nine years I received roughly four thousand bug reports, most of them phrased as demands, several of them threatening, and one, from a hospital network in a city I have never visited, that began with the words "thank you." One. Did any of those four thousand correspondents imagine that a person, rather than a department, was reading them at eleven at night? Alcock understands this loneliness better than any writer I have read, which is precisely why his faith in a check is so puzzling.

¶5 The better cure is already visible in the margins of his own book, though he never names it. The institutions that depend on these libraries do not lack money; they lack a sense that the maintenance is theirs to do. A regional bank runs tidyclock on its login page, employs ninety engineers, and has never assigned one of them a Friday afternoon to review tidyclock's open issues. Volunteer fire departments survive not because the town mails a check to the one person who owns a hose but because the people whose houses would burn show up for the drills. The obligation should attach to dependence, not to profit, and it should be paid in hours, not dollars. This will not rescue every project, and the smallest libraries will still rely on the stubbornness of individuals; but it would spread the weight across the walls that bear it.

¶6 Nobody's Job deserves the wide readership it will probably get. Read it for the first half, which will frighten you in the right way, and argue with the second, which will comfort you in the wrong one. The retired schoolteacher in Pell Harbor did not need a sponsor. She needed the several thousand of us who were standing on her work to notice that we were.

Testimony on Ordinance 14-B

[1] Good evening, members of the Larkhaven City Council. [2] My name is Odile Strand, and I have lived on Quarry Hill Road for twenty-two years. [3] Tonight I want to talk about lights.

[4] Every second Saturday, the Larkhaven Stargazers Club sets up telescopes in the gravel lot behind the public library. [5] Ten years ago, we could show visitors the faint smudge of the Andromeda galaxy without much trouble. [6] Since the city installed the new white LED globes along Cutler Avenue, that smudge has disappeared from our lot entirely. [7] Last spring a nine-year-old girl looked through my eyepiece, saw only a gray haze, and asked whether the telescope was broken.

[8] The problem is not that the lights are on but where they point. [9] The Cutler Avenue fixtures are uncovered globes that throw about a third of their light sideways and upward, where it lights nothing but the sky. [10] The town of Fenwick Ridge, forty miles north, replaced its globes with fully shielded fixtures and reported that its electricity bill for street lighting dropped by 18 percent. pub.passage:
ALTON original passage
Forty Years on 89.7

[1] Radio is a thing that many people have listened to over the years. [2] This Saturday, Riverbend Community Radio turns forty, and its volunteers will spend the weekend asking listeners for enough money to replace a transmitter older than most of its DJs. [3] I think the town should give generously, because the little station on Kettle Street does something no streaming app can do.

[4] Streaming services know what I like, but they do not know where I live. [5] When the Oxbow River flooded in March, it was 89.7 FM that told us which roads were closed and which church basement had dry cots. [6] Volunteer Hal Pruitt stayed on the air for nineteen hours, reading messages from neighbors looking for lost dogs and elderly parents. [7] Every single person in Harrow Bend was listening that night. [8] No algorithm will ever do anything useful for a small town.

[9] The station is also a kind of town square. [10] On Tuesday nights, high school students host a show about their marching band's season, and on Sunday mornings retired farmers argue about rainfall totals. [11] The station's budget is pathetic, and frankly the fact that it survives at all is kind of a joke. [12] Yet it does survive, because ordinary people keep it going.

[13] The pledge drive runs from 6 a.m. Saturday until midnight Sunday, a donation of 25 dollars keeps the station on the air for about an hour. [14] So, that's my opinion on radio.

pub.passage:
ALTON original passage
Who Else Will Come: On Conrad Weil's Siren on the Ridge

¶1 The pager goes off at ten past two in the morning, and for eleven years my first thought was never about the fire but about who else would come. In Brannock County, where I served with the Marrow Creek Volunteer Fire Company until my knees retired me, a structure fire draws whoever is awake, sober, and within fifteen miles. Some nights that is nine people; some nights it is three. Conrad Weil's new book, Siren on the Ridge, is the first account I have read that understands this arithmetic, and it deserves a wide readership among the county commissioners who will decide, over the next decade, whether rural counties keep a volunteer fire service at all.

¶2 Weil's reporting is the book's great strength. He spent two years riding with departments in six counties across three states, and he lets the volunteers speak in their own flat, unsentimental voices. The numbers he gathers are grim: at one station the average age of a responder rose from thirty-four to fifty-seven in twenty years, and the roster shrank from twenty-two names to nine. He describes a chief who answers calls alone because there is no one else, and a township that dissolved its company and now waits forty minutes for an engine from the next county. These are not isolated anecdotes; they are the shape of the thing.

¶3 Where the book falters is in its diagnosis. Weil concludes that the volunteer model is simply obsolete, a relic of a time when men worked within walking distance of the station and could leave the mill when the whistle blew, and he argues that counties should accept the inevitable and hire paid crews. I grant that the old pattern is gone; nobody leaves a shift at a distribution warehouse forty miles away to answer a brush fire. But obsolete is the wrong word for a system that has been quietly loaded with burdens it was never designed to carry. The state now requires one hundred eighty hours of certified training before a recruit may enter a burning building, up from forty when I joined. The company must also buy its own equipment, which means that the same nine people who fight the fires also run the fish fry, the raffle, the mailer, and the pancake breakfast that pays for the air packs. We did not lose volunteers because people stopped caring about their neighbors. We lost them because we asked each one to be a firefighter, a fundraiser, a mechanic, and a grant writer, and then wondered why only retirees had the hours.

¶4 Asking a fire company to sell raffle tickets for its own breathing apparatus is like asking a lifeguard to run a lemonade stand to pay for the pool. The absurdity would be obvious anywhere else. Yet Weil treats the fundraising burden as a charming folkway rather than the structural failure it is, and so he never asks the question that matters: what happens to the roster when the county, not the fish fry, buys the truck?

¶5 We have some evidence, and it is more hopeful than Weil allows. Tillery County, two hours north of us, passed a modest fire levy six years ago, roughly the price of a tank of gas per household per year, and used it to cover equipment and to reimburse recruits for their training hours. Its volunteer roster has grown by a third since, and the average age of a new recruit is twenty-nine. The people were there all along. They had simply been priced out of serving.

¶6 So read Siren on the Ridge for its portraits, which are honest and often moving, and for its warning, which is overdue. But read it skeptically when it reaches for the obituary. Volunteer fire service is not dying of old age; it is being starved, and starvation, unlike age, has a remedy. If you sit on a county board, the remedy is in your budget. The pager will go off tonight somewhere in your district, and the only question that matters is who else will come.

ALTON original passage
Forty Years on 89.7

[1] Radio is a thing that many people have listened to over the years. [2] This Saturday, Riverbend Community Radio turns forty, and its volunteers will spend the weekend asking listeners for enough money to replace a transmitter older than most of its DJs. [3] I think the town should give generously, because the little station on Kettle Street does something no streaming app can do.

[4] Streaming services know what I like, but they do not know where I live. [5] When the Oxbow River flooded in March, it was 89.7 FM that told us which roads were closed and which church basement had dry cots. [6] Volunteer Hal Pruitt stayed on the air for nineteen hours, reading messages from neighbors looking for lost dogs and elderly parents. [7] Every single person in Harrow Bend was listening that night. [8] No algorithm will ever do anything useful for a small town.

[9] The station is also a kind of town square. [10] On Tuesday nights, high school students host a show about their marching band's season, and on Sunday mornings retired farmers argue about rainfall totals. [11] The station's budget is pathetic, and frankly the fact that it survives at all is kind of a joke. [12] Yet it does survive, because ordinary people keep it going.

[13] The pledge drive runs from 6 a.m. Saturday until midnight Sunday, a donation of 25 dollars keeps the station on the air for about an hour. [14] So, that's my opinion on radio.

Forty Years on 89.7

[1] Radio is a thing that many people have listened to over the years. [2] This Saturday, Riverbend Community Radio turns forty, and its volunteers will spend the weekend asking listeners for enough money to replace a transmitter older than most of its DJs. [3] I think the town should give generously, because the little station on Kettle Street does something no streaming app can do.

[4] Streaming services know what I like, but they do not know where I live. [5] When the Oxbow River flooded in March, it was 89.7 FM that told us which roads were closed and which church basement had dry cots. [6] Volunteer Hal Pruitt stayed on the air for nineteen hours, reading messages from neighbors looking for lost dogs and elderly parents. [7] Every single person in Harrow Bend was listening that night. [8] No algorithm will ever do anything useful for a small town.

[9] The station is also a kind of town square. [10] On Tuesday nights, high school students host a show about their marching band's season, and on Sunday mornings retired farmers argue about rainfall totals. [11] The station's budget is pathetic, and frankly the fact that it survives at all is kind of a joke. [12] Yet it does survive, because ordinary people keep it going.

[13] The pledge drive runs from 6 a.m. Saturday until midnight Sunday, a donation of 25 dollars keeps the station on the air for about an hour. [14] So, that's my opinion on radio.

pub.passage:
ALTON original passage
The Drift Was Never the Interesting Part

¶1 I want to start with a morning in late January, two winters ago, because it is the morning people imagine when they hear that I ride a bicycle to work all year. It was eleven below zero at the bridge, cold enough that the chain ticked like a cooling engine, and the river path had not been plowed. I walked the bike a mile and a half through shin-deep snow and arrived at the clinic forty minutes late. That is the picture: a stubborn woman dragging a machine through a drift. I am here tonight to tell you that the picture is accurate and that it is also almost entirely beside the point.

¶2 Of the roughly one hundred and ten working days between November and March, that morning was one of perhaps four I would call genuinely bad. The others were simply cold, which is a different thing. Cold is a problem of clothing; snow is a problem of maintenance; and only the first of these is mine to solve. When I say winter commuting, I do not mean an expedition. I mean a twenty-two-minute ride on studded tires, a pair of mittens that cost less than a tank of gasoline, and a path that somebody has cleared. Remove that last item and the whole arrangement collapses, not because the riders are weak but because nobody can pedal through a foot of unplowed snow, any more than you can drive through it.

¶3 I know what some of you are thinking, because I have heard it at this forum before: that the riders are a handful of enthusiasts, and that a city of thirty thousand cannot justify a plow for a few dozen people in reflective jackets. It is a fair objection, and I want to take it seriously rather than wave it away. The count is low because the path is unreliable, and the path is unreliable because the count is low; the city has built itself a circle and then pointed at the circle as proof. Last winter, when Public Works kept the path cleared for six weeks as a trial, the counter at the Hollis Street bridge recorded an average of ninety-one riders a day, up from nineteen the year before. Nobody bought new bicycles in February. Those riders were already here, waiting for the city to decide whether they existed.

¶4 Consider how we treat the sidewalk. We do not ask whether enough people walk on Fenwick Avenue in January to justify shoveling it; we assume that a sidewalk under snow is a failure of the city, not a verdict on pedestrians. A bicycle path is a sidewalk with a longer stride. It carries the nurse, the night-shift baker, the ninth-grader too young to drive whose parents both leave the house before seven. Those people do not stop needing to get across town when the temperature drops; they simply stop being counted.

¶5 Let me be honest about the limits of what I am asking. There will be mornings, four or five a winter, when the plow cannot keep up and nobody should be on the path, and I am not asking the city to promise otherwise. I am asking for something smaller and duller: that the river path go on the same plowing schedule as the residential streets, which by Public Works' own estimate would add about eleven thousand dollars a year to a snow budget of just under two million. That is less than the cost of one of the salt trucks parked behind this building.

¶6 So here is the picture I would rather you carry out of this room tonight. Not a woman hauling a bicycle through a drift, but a cleared path at seven in the morning, a few tail-lights blinking red against the snow, the baker and the nurse and the ninth-grader going to work in the ordinary way, in a town that decided they were worth a plow. The drift was never the interesting part. The interesting part is what the town does about it.

pub.passage:
ALTON original passage
A Fence Around an Hour

¶1 The pledge card came in the same envelope as the library's autumn newsletter, printed on oatmeal-colored stock with a line for each member of the household to sign. "Screens Down at Supper," it read, and underneath, in smaller type, "Give your children back the table." I read it twice at my own kitchen table, phone face down beside the sugar bowl, and felt the particular unease of someone who agrees with a proposal and distrusts its wording. Give the children back the table? Who, exactly, had taken it from them?

¶2 My grandmother, Solveig Arnesen, bought her first radio in the autumn of 1938, a walnut cabinet set that cost her, according to the household ledger she kept in a looping hand, thirty-one dollars and forty cents. The ledger records the purchase on a Tuesday. By the following Sunday a second entry appears, not a sum but a sentence: "No set from six to seven. All of us." The family story is that my grandfather, not the children, had been the trouble, sitting with his ear to the speaker through an entire meal while the program crackled about grain prices and a prizefight in a city none of them would ever see. The rule she wrote was not a punishment for the young. It was a fence she built around an hour, and she built it to keep herself and her husband inside as much as anyone.

¶3 The pattern repeated itself with a regularity that would be comic if it were not so instructive. In 1954 the telephone arrived, and my mother remembers the cord unplugged at a quarter to six and coiled on top of the icebox like a sleeping cat. In 1967 the television came, and with it a new entry in a new ledger, this time in my mother's hand: "Set off at supper, no exceptions, Dad included." Each machine was a stranger at the door, and each time the household did the same thing: it did not bar the stranger, it told the stranger when to call. The radio stayed; the telephone stayed; the television, heaven help us, stayed. What changed was that a single hour was marked off as belonging to the people at the table rather than to the voices coming through the wall.

¶4 There is a difference, I think, between a curfew and a ritual, and the difference matters more than the hour chosen. A curfew is a rule imposed on someone by someone else; it names a suspect and a warden. A ritual is a thing a group does together, on purpose, at a set time, because doing it together is the point. The mill at the foot of Carrow Bend used to blow its whistle at noon, and nobody heard that whistle as an accusation; it was simply the sound of everyone stopping at once. My grandmother's "All of us" was a whistle, not a warrant.

¶5 I will concede that the ledgers do not record a single happy supper. They record cabbage and coal and the price of shoes, and the surviving letters mention more than one meal eaten in a silence that was sullen rather than peaceful, teenagers and tired parents with nothing to say and a forbidden radio in the next room. Nostalgia would have me believe that the quiet hour produced conversation; the evidence suggests only that it produced attendance. But attendance, it turns out, is not nothing. The sullen suppers of 1941 are the ones my mother still describes in detail, down to the pattern on the oilcloth, and she cannot describe a single evening when the set was on.

¶6 So I will sign the card, and I would urge you to sign it as well, though I would ask you to take a pen and cross out the second line before you do. Do not give the children back the table. Sit down at it yourself, phone in the drawer, and let them see you, every night, until the hour belongs to all of you and nobody remembers whom it was meant to protect. My grandmother knew this in 1938 with a radio she could barely afford. The machine has changed. The fence has not.

pub.passage:
ALTON original source — a summary of a (fictional) peer-reviewed study.

Sleep Duration and Daily Mood in Ninth Graders

Introduction
Many teenagers sleep less than experts recommend. This study examined the hypothesis that ninth graders who sleep longer on school nights report better mood the next day than ninth graders who sleep less.

Participants
The 240 participants were ninth graders at one suburban high school. Of the 400 students who were invited, 240 returned both a parent permission form and their own signed agreement, and they were included in the study.

Procedure
Each student wore a wrist sleep monitor for 14 school nights. The monitor recorded the minutes between falling asleep and waking up. Each morning students rated their mood on a scale from 1 (very bad) to 10 (very good) in a phone app. Sleep duration was defined as each student's average number of minutes of sleep per night across the 14 nights, and mood was defined as each student's average morning rating across the 14 days.

Ethical procedures
A university institutional review board approved the study. Students' data were stored under code numbers, and only the research team could link codes to names. Students were told they could leave the study at any time and that the school would not see any individual's data.

Results
The researchers calculated a correlation coefficient between average sleep duration and average mood rating. The table shows the results.

pub.passage:
ALTON original source — a summary of a (fictional) peer-reviewed study.

Practice Quizzes and Retention of Science Vocabulary in Seventh Graders

Introduction
Teachers often ask students to reread a text to prepare for a test. Research on memory suggests that practicing retrieval may help more than rereading. In this study, researchers tested the hypothesis that taking a practice quiz leads to better retention of science vocabulary than rereading the same material.

Participants
The 120 participants were seventh graders from two public middle schools in one mid-sized city. All students whose parents returned a permission form and who agreed to take part were included. A computer randomly assigned the students to the Quiz group (60 students) or the Reread group (60 students).

Procedure
All students studied a 20-term science vocabulary text for 15 minutes. The Quiz group then spent 10 minutes taking a practice quiz on the terms, and the Reread group spent 10 minutes rereading the text. One week later, all students took a 20-item test in which they wrote the definition of each term. Retention was defined as the number of the 20 terms that a student defined correctly on the one-week test.

Ethical procedures
The study was approved by the school district's institutional review board. Parents gave written permission, and each student gave verbal agreement and was told that he or she could stop at any time without penalty. Students' tests were labeled with code numbers rather than names.

Results
The table shows the results. The researchers reported that the difference between the groups was statistically significant.

ALTON original passage
The Six, 1963 to 2024

¶1 The Number 6 crosstown bus died last Saturday at 11:42 in the evening, at the corner of Pell Street and Mills Avenue, after a long illness that its physicians called a budget. It was sixty-one years old. It is survived by a fleet of ride-hailing sedans, a pilot program of on-demand shuttles, and roughly four thousand regular passengers who have not yet decided what to do on Monday. I rode the last run, as did a retired dispatcher named Orrin Belcastro, who brought a folding chair in case the seats were full. They were.

¶2 An obituary is supposed to tell you what a life was for, and so I will try. The Six was never fast; its route bent like a river to touch the hospital, the community college, the cannery district, and the three blocks of Hadley Avenue where the bakeries open before dawn. Planners in the 1990s called this bend an inefficiency. The people who rode it called it the reason they rode it. A transit line is not a pipe for moving bodies from one point to another; it is a public room on wheels, and a room is judged by who can get into it.

¶3 Consider the ledger the city's consultants prepared last spring. They found that the Six recovered only 23 percent of its operating cost from fares, compared with 41 percent on the express routes that run from the suburbs to the financial district. The number is accurate, and I do not dispute it. But notice what the number cannot see: the nursing assistant who kept her job at Mercy Ridge because the 5:10 bus was reliable, the sophomore who finished her degree because she never had to buy a car, the widower on Pell Street who rode to the end of the line and back every Tuesday simply to be among people. Fares are what a bus collects; they are not what a bus produces.

¶4 I will concede that nostalgia makes a poor transportation policy. Some of the Six's riders will be served well enough by the on-demand shuttles, which can be summoned by telephone and which, on paper, cover the same territory. If the shuttles turn out to be prompt and cheap, I will say so in this column. Yet a service that must be requested is not the same as a service that simply arrives. The bus did not ask who you were, whether your phone was charged, or whether you had the English to explain your destination to a dispatcher; it pulled up, opened its doors, and waited the same eleven seconds for everyone.

¶5 Mr. Belcastro told me, somewhere near the cannery, about the winter of the ice storm, when the Six was the only vehicle on the Mills Avenue bridge for three days and the drivers ran it without collecting fares because the fareboxes had frozen. Nobody ordered them to. He said it the way some men talk about a war they were proud to have served in: not boasting, just reporting. That is what an institution is: a habit of service that outlasts the memo that created it.

¶6 When the bus reached the Pell Street terminus, the driver, a woman named Luz Arrieta who had held the route for nineteen years, did not announce anything. She set the brake, opened both doors, and let the silence do the work. Then somebody in the back began to applaud, and the sound moved forward through the bus the way warmth moves through a cold room, unevenly and then all at once. We will be told, in the coming months, that Calloway has modernized. Perhaps it has. But a city that cannot keep a bus running for the people who cannot keep a car is not modern; it is merely unaccompanied. The Six is gone, and the question it answered every day, who is this place for, is now open again.

pub.passage:
ALTON original passage
What Your Phone Doesn't Know About Our Clay

[1] Every Saturday at the Hollins Lane Community Garden, someone asks why their tomatoes split, and every Saturday someone else answers by holding up a phone. [2] I am Ruth Okafor-Lind, I tend plot 14, and I want to make a case for a building most of us drive right past: the Pell Street Branch Library. [3] Libraries are good things to have in a town.

[4] A search engine gives you answers in a hurry, but it does not know our soil. [5] Our clay holds water for days, and advice written for sandy coastal gardens can drown a seedling here. [6] Pell Street keeps local knowledge that no search result can match. [7] Last spring I asked a librarian there, Mr. Dowd, about blossom-end rot, and he pulled out a county pamphlet from 1987 and a binder of notes left by a gardener who worked this same lot forty years ago.

[8] Search engines are completely useless for gardeners and should never be trusted. [9] Last year, the branch also began lending seeds from an old wooden card catalog near the front desk. [10] Gardeners borrow a packet in April, and in the fall they return seeds saved from their strongest plants. [11] The reason why this is important is because of the fact that the seeds that come back each year are seeds that have already proven that they can survive in our clay and our short summers.

[12] The county board votes on the library's budget on March 9. [13] Board members have proposed cutting the branch's Saturday hours, the only hours many working gardeners can visit, and the plan would close it's seed desk on weekends. [14] If you have ever borrowed a seed packet, a book, or a librarian's patience, come to the meeting and say so.

pub.passage:
ALTON original passage
Sixty-One Sycamores

¶1 When I was twenty-three and newly hired by the town of Harrow Fen, my supervisor handed me a clipboard and told me to count the trees on Calder Avenue. I assumed it was busywork. It took four days, because every sycamore on that street had something to say: a hollow where a raccoon had raised three litters, a lightning scar healed over like a closed eye, a root that had lifted a sidewalk slab and then, with a patience I did not yet understand, grown around it. Graduates, I have been asked to speak to you about your futures, and I intend to, but I am going to do it by talking about those sycamores, because last Tuesday the council voted to widen Calder Avenue, and the plan calls for removing all sixty-one of them.

¶2 Let me be precise about what we mean when we say old-growth on a city street, since the phrase was borrowed from forestry and does not fit perfectly. In a forest, old growth describes a stand that has never been cleared. On a street, it describes something rarer: a tree that has survived a century of paving, trenching, salt, and committees. Every one of those sycamores was planted by a person who knew they would never sit in its shade. That is not sentiment; that is the definition.

¶3 You have spent years learning to call things by their proper names, so call a street tree what it is: infrastructure. A storm sewer carries water away; a mature sycamore intercepts roughly three thousand gallons of rainfall a year before it ever reaches the sewer. A transformer cools a block in August; the canopy on Calder lowers surface temperature by double digits, according to the thermal survey our own department commissioned seven years ago. We do not demolish a bridge because it is old. We inspect it, we repair it, and when we must, we close a lane. Yet the same council that budgets forty years of maintenance for a culvert will vote to erase a hundred and forty years of canopy in an afternoon, because a tree, unlike a culvert, does not appear on the balance sheet as an asset that depreciates.

¶4 I will concede the obvious. Some old trees must come down. I have signed the removal orders myself, standing under a red oak with a fungal rot that had eaten two-thirds of its heartwood, and I did not sleep well afterward, but I signed. A dangerous tree is not a monument; it is a liability with leaves. But the Calder sycamores are not dangerous. The widening is proposed so that traffic can move eleven seconds faster at the Pell Street light. Eleven seconds. We are being asked to trade a century for a fraction of a minute, and to call the trade progress.

¶5 So here is what I am asking of you, and it is harder than it sounds. You will be the ones in the room when the next Calder Avenue comes up for a vote. You will have the drawings, the models, the cost estimates, and you will be tempted to treat a mature tree the way the software treats it: as a circle on a plan, easily erased and easily redrawn somewhere else. Resist that. A sapling planted in mitigation is not a replacement; it is an IOU that will not be paid during your career, or your children's. Insist that the removal of an old-growth street tree be justified the way we justify closing a hospital wing: reluctantly, publicly, and with the arithmetic on the table.

¶6 I counted sixty-one sycamores in my first week of work. I would like to count them again at the end of yours. Go and be the kind of planners who make that possible.

ALTON original passage
Keep Quarry Street Slow

[1] Last Tuesday I walked from my house on Linden Row to the Quarry Street bakery, a trip of eleven minutes that I have made almost every morning for twenty years. [2] Along the way I waved to the crossing guard, traded tomato seedlings with Mr. Abernathy, and stopped to read a notice taped to a lamppost. [3] It announced that on March 14 the council will vote on a plan to widen Quarry Street to four lanes, which would remove the benches and shrink the sidewalks to three feet. [4] Walkability is something that really matters a lot.

[5] Quarry Street is a place where people move slowly. [6] When Rosa Delgado put two benches outside her hardware store in 2019, she says her weekday sales rose by nearly a third. [7] Marguerite Osei, who runs the bakery, told me her sidewalk tables did the same for her morning trade. [8] Any traffic engineer who wants to widen this street has obviously never bothered to walk down it.

[9] Supporters of the plan point out that commuters from the new Birchfield subdivision lose about ten minutes a day waiting at the Quarry Street light. [10] That is a real cost, and I do not dismiss it. [11] But a wider street would move those drivers through our neighborhood faster, it would also give them less reason to ever stop in it. [12] I urge readers to come to the council meeting on March 14 and speak up for the sidewalks.

pub.passage:
ALTON original passage
A Fence Around an Hour

¶1 The pledge card came in the same envelope as the library's autumn newsletter, printed on oatmeal-colored stock with a line for each member of the household to sign. "Screens Down at Supper," it read, and underneath, in smaller type, "Give your children back the table." I read it twice at my own kitchen table, phone face down beside the sugar bowl, and felt the particular unease of someone who agrees with a proposal and distrusts its wording. Give the children back the table? Who, exactly, had taken it from them?

¶2 My grandmother, Solveig Arnesen, bought her first radio in the autumn of 1938, a walnut cabinet set that cost her, according to the household ledger she kept in a looping hand, thirty-one dollars and forty cents. The ledger records the purchase on a Tuesday. By the following Sunday a second entry appears, not a sum but a sentence: "No set from six to seven. All of us." The family story is that my grandfather, not the children, had been the trouble, sitting with his ear to the speaker through an entire meal while the program crackled about grain prices and a prizefight in a city none of them would ever see. The rule she wrote was not a punishment for the young. It was a fence she built around an hour, and she built it to keep herself and her husband inside as much as anyone.

¶3 The pattern repeated itself with a regularity that would be comic if it were not so instructive. In 1954 the telephone arrived, and my mother remembers the cord unplugged at a quarter to six and coiled on top of the icebox like a sleeping cat. In 1967 the television came, and with it a new entry in a new ledger, this time in my mother's hand: "Set off at supper, no exceptions, Dad included." Each machine was a stranger at the door, and each time the household did the same thing: it did not bar the stranger, it told the stranger when to call. The radio stayed; the telephone stayed; the television, heaven help us, stayed. What changed was that a single hour was marked off as belonging to the people at the table rather than to the voices coming through the wall.

¶4 There is a difference, I think, between a curfew and a ritual, and the difference matters more than the hour chosen. A curfew is a rule imposed on someone by someone else; it names a suspect and a warden. A ritual is a thing a group does together, on purpose, at a set time, because doing it together is the point. The mill at the foot of Carrow Bend used to blow its whistle at noon, and nobody heard that whistle as an accusation; it was simply the sound of everyone stopping at once. My grandmother's "All of us" was a whistle, not a warrant.

¶5 I will concede that the ledgers do not record a single happy supper. They record cabbage and coal and the price of shoes, and the surviving letters mention more than one meal eaten in a silence that was sullen rather than peaceful, teenagers and tired parents with nothing to say and a forbidden radio in the next room. Nostalgia would have me believe that the quiet hour produced conversation; the evidence suggests only that it produced attendance. But attendance, it turns out, is not nothing. The sullen suppers of 1941 are the ones my mother still describes in detail, down to the pattern on the oilcloth, and she cannot describe a single evening when the set was on.

¶6 So I will sign the card, and I would urge you to sign it as well, though I would ask you to take a pen and cross out the second line before you do. Do not give the children back the table. Sit down at it yourself, phone in the drawer, and let them see you, every night, until the hour belongs to all of you and nobody remembers whom it was meant to protect. My grandmother knew this in 1938 with a radio she could barely afford. The machine has changed. The fence has not.

pub.passage:
ALTON original passage
Who Else Will Come: On Conrad Weil's Siren on the Ridge

¶1 The pager goes off at ten past two in the morning, and for eleven years my first thought was never about the fire but about who else would come. In Brannock County, where I served with the Marrow Creek Volunteer Fire Company until my knees retired me, a structure fire draws whoever is awake, sober, and within fifteen miles. Some nights that is nine people; some nights it is three. Conrad Weil's new book, Siren on the Ridge, is the first account I have read that understands this arithmetic, and it deserves a wide readership among the county commissioners who will decide, over the next decade, whether rural counties keep a volunteer fire service at all.

¶2 Weil's reporting is the book's great strength. He spent two years riding with departments in six counties across three states, and he lets the volunteers speak in their own flat, unsentimental voices. The numbers he gathers are grim: at one station the average age of a responder rose from thirty-four to fifty-seven in twenty years, and the roster shrank from twenty-two names to nine. He describes a chief who answers calls alone because there is no one else, and a township that dissolved its company and now waits forty minutes for an engine from the next county. These are not isolated anecdotes; they are the shape of the thing.

¶3 Where the book falters is in its diagnosis. Weil concludes that the volunteer model is simply obsolete, a relic of a time when men worked within walking distance of the station and could leave the mill when the whistle blew, and he argues that counties should accept the inevitable and hire paid crews. I grant that the old pattern is gone; nobody leaves a shift at a distribution warehouse forty miles away to answer a brush fire. But obsolete is the wrong word for a system that has been quietly loaded with burdens it was never designed to carry. The state now requires one hundred eighty hours of certified training before a recruit may enter a burning building, up from forty when I joined. The company must also buy its own equipment, which means that the same nine people who fight the fires also run the fish fry, the raffle, the mailer, and the pancake breakfast that pays for the air packs. We did not lose volunteers because people stopped caring about their neighbors. We lost them because we asked each one to be a firefighter, a fundraiser, a mechanic, and a grant writer, and then wondered why only retirees had the hours.

¶4 Asking a fire company to sell raffle tickets for its own breathing apparatus is like asking a lifeguard to run a lemonade stand to pay for the pool. The absurdity would be obvious anywhere else. Yet Weil treats the fundraising burden as a charming folkway rather than the structural failure it is, and so he never asks the question that matters: what happens to the roster when the county, not the fish fry, buys the truck?

¶5 We have some evidence, and it is more hopeful than Weil allows. Tillery County, two hours north of us, passed a modest fire levy six years ago, roughly the price of a tank of gas per household per year, and used it to cover equipment and to reimburse recruits for their training hours. Its volunteer roster has grown by a third since, and the average age of a new recruit is twenty-nine. The people were there all along. They had simply been priced out of serving.

¶6 So read Siren on the Ridge for its portraits, which are honest and often moving, and for its warning, which is overdue. But read it skeptically when it reaches for the obituary. Volunteer fire service is not dying of old age; it is being starved, and starvation, unlike age, has a remedy. If you sit on a county board, the remedy is in your budget. The pager will go off tonight somewhere in your district, and the only question that matters is who else will come.

pub.passage:
ALTON original passage
The Hand That Drew It: Remembering Teodora Quist

¶1 Teodora Quist kept a jar of eraser crumbs on her drafting table and told every new apprentice that it was the most honest record of her career. She died last month in Lower Marrow at eighty-one, in the house behind the county survey office where she had drawn maps for forty-three years. She taught a generation of us that a map is not a picture of the world. It is a case made about the world, built with the same tools as any other case: selection, emphasis, and omission.

¶2 Most people would say a map is a drawing that shows where things are. Quist would say it is a drawing that shows which things the mapmaker decided you should know are there. A sheet of paper cannot hold a county; it holds perhaps a thousandth of what a county contains, and the rest must be left off. Every blank space, she liked to say, is a verdict. The road drawn thick and the stream drawn thin, the village named and the settlement unnamed, the boundary inked solid and the boundary left dotted: these are not observations but rulings.

¶3 The clearest demonstration came when the Marrow County Board asked her office for a map to accompany a vote on building along the river's lower terrace. Standard practice would have been to shade the floodplain in the pale blue the state style guide recommended, a blue so gentle it reads as decoration. Quist shaded it in a mud brown no one could mistake for ornament, and she printed the crest of the 1961 flood at every bridge. The developers' attorney called the map inflammatory. She answered that the pale blue was also inflammatory; it simply inflamed in the other direction. The board voted nine to two against the project, and three members later said the brown was what they remembered when they voted.

¶4 Her critics, and she had them, said this proved she was an advocate who happened to own a drafting pen rather than a surveyor who happened to have opinions. I will grant them half of that. She did want the project stopped, and she said so to anyone who asked. But the charge assumes that somewhere a map exists with no advocate behind it, a sheet that merely reports, and in forty-three years she never saw one and neither have I. The pale blue floodplain had an advocate too; he was just quieter about it. What distinguished Quist was not that her maps argued but that she signed the argument.

¶5 She trained apprentices with a single exercise, repeated until it became reflex. Given one set of survey data for a single square mile, we drew three maps: one for a family thinking of buying a house there, one for a company planning a pipeline, and one for a child who would walk to school along its lanes. The data never changed. The maps never matched. The buyer's map grew contour lines and drainage; the pipeline's map grew easements and bedrock; the child's map grew crossings, dogs, and the one hedge you could cut through. After the third round, nobody could say "just the facts" with a straight face, which was, I think, the whole point.

¶6 The week after she died I went to the survey office, mostly to sit in the chair, and the jar of eraser crumbs was still there, fuller than I remembered. It struck me that she had kept it because it was, in its way, her finest map: a record of every line she had chosen, on reflection, not to let stand. We will mourn her, and we will do it properly. But I would ask anyone reading this, the next time a map is unfolded at a council meeting or on a phone screen, to do what she did and look first for the hand that drew it. Ask what it was told to show you. Then ask what it was told to leave out.

pub.passage:
ALTON original passage
Forty Years on 89.7

[1] Radio is a thing that many people have listened to over the years. [2] This Saturday, Riverbend Community Radio turns forty, and its volunteers will spend the weekend asking listeners for enough money to replace a transmitter older than most of its DJs. [3] I think the town should give generously, because the little station on Kettle Street does something no streaming app can do.

[4] Streaming services know what I like, but they do not know where I live. [5] When the Oxbow River flooded in March, it was 89.7 FM that told us which roads were closed and which church basement had dry cots. [6] Volunteer Hal Pruitt stayed on the air for nineteen hours, reading messages from neighbors looking for lost dogs and elderly parents. [7] Every single person in Harrow Bend was listening that night. [8] No algorithm will ever do anything useful for a small town.

[9] The station is also a kind of town square. [10] On Tuesday nights, high school students host a show about their marching band's season, and on Sunday mornings retired farmers argue about rainfall totals. [11] The station's budget is pathetic, and frankly the fact that it survives at all is kind of a joke. [12] Yet it does survive, because ordinary people keep it going.

[13] The pledge drive runs from 6 a.m. Saturday until midnight Sunday, a donation of 25 dollars keeps the station on the air for about an hour. [14] So, that's my opinion on radio.

pub.passage:
ALTON original passage
Eight Bars at the Grange Hall

[1] Last Thursday I sat in the back row of the Fenwick Grange Hall while the Marrow Creek Community Orchestra rehearsed for its spring concert. [2] Orchestras are interesting and say a lot about people. [3] Forty-one players showed up, from a fourteen-year-old violist to a retired mail carrier who has played second trombone for thirty years.

[4] Conductor Abel Ostrander stopped the group six times in the first piece, each time over the same eight bars. [5] The flutes were rushing, the cellos were dragging, and nobody could hear the oboe. [6] Ostrander did not single anyone out; instead, he asked every section except the oboe to play the passage half as loud. [7] By the fourth try, the oboe melody floated clearly over the whole ensemble. [8] Every musician in an orchestra always cares more about the group than about his or her own part.

[9] During the break, the cellists told me their section meets on Sunday afternoons to work through tricky passages together. [10] Players share music stands, and the woodwinds carry spare reeds for anyone who forgets theirs. [11] The orchestra holds no auditions, anyone who can read music is welcome. [12] Our town council, which spent last winter arguing over a parking lot could learn something from them.

[13] Anyway, that is what I saw at the rehearsal.

pub.passage:
ALTON original passage
Sixty-One Sycamores

¶1 When I was twenty-three and newly hired by the town of Harrow Fen, my supervisor handed me a clipboard and told me to count the trees on Calder Avenue. I assumed it was busywork. It took four days, because every sycamore on that street had something to say: a hollow where a raccoon had raised three litters, a lightning scar healed over like a closed eye, a root that had lifted a sidewalk slab and then, with a patience I did not yet understand, grown around it. Graduates, I have been asked to speak to you about your futures, and I intend to, but I am going to do it by talking about those sycamores, because last Tuesday the council voted to widen Calder Avenue, and the plan calls for removing all sixty-one of them.

¶2 Let me be precise about what we mean when we say old-growth on a city street, since the phrase was borrowed from forestry and does not fit perfectly. In a forest, old growth describes a stand that has never been cleared. On a street, it describes something rarer: a tree that has survived a century of paving, trenching, salt, and committees. Every one of those sycamores was planted by a person who knew they would never sit in its shade. That is not sentiment; that is the definition.

¶3 You have spent years learning to call things by their proper names, so call a street tree what it is: infrastructure. A storm sewer carries water away; a mature sycamore intercepts roughly three thousand gallons of rainfall a year before it ever reaches the sewer. A transformer cools a block in August; the canopy on Calder lowers surface temperature by double digits, according to the thermal survey our own department commissioned seven years ago. We do not demolish a bridge because it is old. We inspect it, we repair it, and when we must, we close a lane. Yet the same council that budgets forty years of maintenance for a culvert will vote to erase a hundred and forty years of canopy in an afternoon, because a tree, unlike a culvert, does not appear on the balance sheet as an asset that depreciates.

¶4 I will concede the obvious. Some old trees must come down. I have signed the removal orders myself, standing under a red oak with a fungal rot that had eaten two-thirds of its heartwood, and I did not sleep well afterward, but I signed. A dangerous tree is not a monument; it is a liability with leaves. But the Calder sycamores are not dangerous. The widening is proposed so that traffic can move eleven seconds faster at the Pell Street light. Eleven seconds. We are being asked to trade a century for a fraction of a minute, and to call the trade progress.

¶5 So here is what I am asking of you, and it is harder than it sounds. You will be the ones in the room when the next Calder Avenue comes up for a vote. You will have the drawings, the models, the cost estimates, and you will be tempted to treat a mature tree the way the software treats it: as a circle on a plan, easily erased and easily redrawn somewhere else. Resist that. A sapling planted in mitigation is not a replacement; it is an IOU that will not be paid during your career, or your children's. Insist that the removal of an old-growth street tree be justified the way we justify closing a hospital wing: reluctantly, publicly, and with the arithmetic on the table.

¶6 I counted sixty-one sycamores in my first week of work. I would like to count them again at the end of yours. Go and be the kind of planners who make that possible.

ALTON original passage
Forty Years on 89.7

[1] Radio is a thing that many people have listened to over the years. [2] This Saturday, Riverbend Community Radio turns forty, and its volunteers will spend the weekend asking listeners for enough money to replace a transmitter older than most of its DJs. [3] I think the town should give generously, because the little station on Kettle Street does something no streaming app can do.

[4] Streaming services know what I like, but they do not know where I live. [5] When the Oxbow River flooded in March, it was 89.7 FM that told us which roads were closed and which church basement had dry cots. [6] Volunteer Hal Pruitt stayed on the air for nineteen hours, reading messages from neighbors looking for lost dogs and elderly parents. [7] Every single person in Harrow Bend was listening that night. [8] No algorithm will ever do anything useful for a small town.

[9] The station is also a kind of town square. [10] On Tuesday nights, high school students host a show about their marching band's season, and on Sunday mornings retired farmers argue about rainfall totals. [11] The station's budget is pathetic, and frankly the fact that it survives at all is kind of a joke. [12] Yet it does survive, because ordinary people keep it going.

[13] The pledge drive runs from 6 a.m. Saturday until midnight Sunday, a donation of 25 dollars keeps the station on the air for about an hour. [14] So, that's my opinion on radio.

ALTON original passage
What Your Phone Doesn't Know About Our Clay

[1] Every Saturday at the Hollins Lane Community Garden, someone asks why their tomatoes split, and every Saturday someone else answers by holding up a phone. [2] I am Ruth Okafor-Lind, I tend plot 14, and I want to make a case for a building most of us drive right past: the Pell Street Branch Library. [3] Libraries are good things to have in a town.

[4] A search engine gives you answers in a hurry, but it does not know our soil. [5] Our clay holds water for days, and advice written for sandy coastal gardens can drown a seedling here. [6] Pell Street keeps local knowledge that no search result can match. [7] Last spring I asked a librarian there, Mr. Dowd, about blossom-end rot, and he pulled out a county pamphlet from 1987 and a binder of notes left by a gardener who worked this same lot forty years ago.

[8] Search engines are completely useless for gardeners and should never be trusted. [9] Last year, the branch also began lending seeds from an old wooden card catalog near the front desk. [10] Gardeners borrow a packet in April, and in the fall they return seeds saved from their strongest plants. [11] The reason why this is important is because of the fact that the seeds that come back each year are seeds that have already proven that they can survive in our clay and our short summers.

[12] The county board votes on the library's budget on March 9. [13] Board members have proposed cutting the branch's Saturday hours, the only hours many working gardeners can visit, and the plan would close it's seed desk on weekends. [14] If you have ever borrowed a seed packet, a book, or a librarian's patience, come to the meeting and say so.

pub.passage:
ALTON original passage
Standing on Her Work

¶1 One Tuesday last October, a date-formatting library called tidyclock vanished from the public package registry, and by morning several thousand websites could no longer tell their users what day it was. Its sole maintainer, a retired schoolteacher in Pell Harbor, had deleted it after a decade of unpaid work and one rude bug report too many. Desmond Alcock's new book, Nobody's Job, opens with that night, and it is the right place to begin. I spent nine years maintaining a small text-parsing library used by companies I was never allowed to name, so I read Alcock with the uneasy attention of a patient reading her own chart.

¶2 The book's first half is a diagnosis, and it is a good one. Alcock surveyed four hundred of the most heavily downloaded packages in three programming languages and found that more than half depended on a single active volunteer. He calls these projects load-bearing walls that no inspector has visited, and the metaphor earns its keep: the walls are hidden inside the plaster of every bank, hospital, and school district that runs code on top of them. Nobody chose this arrangement. It accreted, one convenient download at a time, until the whole structure rested on the patience of people who could stop at any moment and owed us nothing if they did.

¶3 It is in the second half, where Alcock turns from diagnosis to cure, that the book loses its footing. His remedy is sponsorship: corporations that profit from open-source software should fund its maintainers, and he describes several foundations that already do so. I will grant that money has saved projects. A stipend kept at least one widely used encryption library alive after its maintainer nearly quit, and Alcock tells that story well. But a stipend changes what the work is. Consider the neighbor who shovels the shared walkway every winter because no one else will; the day you start paying her, the shoveling becomes a service, the snow becomes her problem, and you acquire the right to complain about ice. Sponsorship converts a gift into a contract, and the contract arrives written in the sponsor's priorities, not the project's.

¶4 I know something about how such gifts are received. In nine years I received roughly four thousand bug reports, most of them phrased as demands, several of them threatening, and one, from a hospital network in a city I have never visited, that began with the words "thank you." One. Did any of those four thousand correspondents imagine that a person, rather than a department, was reading them at eleven at night? Alcock understands this loneliness better than any writer I have read, which is precisely why his faith in a check is so puzzling.

¶5 The better cure is already visible in the margins of his own book, though he never names it. The institutions that depend on these libraries do not lack money; they lack a sense that the maintenance is theirs to do. A regional bank runs tidyclock on its login page, employs ninety engineers, and has never assigned one of them a Friday afternoon to review tidyclock's open issues. Volunteer fire departments survive not because the town mails a check to the one person who owns a hose but because the people whose houses would burn show up for the drills. The obligation should attach to dependence, not to profit, and it should be paid in hours, not dollars. This will not rescue every project, and the smallest libraries will still rely on the stubbornness of individuals; but it would spread the weight across the walls that bear it.

¶6 Nobody's Job deserves the wide readership it will probably get. Read it for the first half, which will frighten you in the right way, and argue with the second, which will comfort you in the wrong one. The retired schoolteacher in Pell Harbor did not need a sponsor. She needed the several thousand of us who were standing on her work to notice that we were.

What the Shoreline Taught Us: A Report on Merrow Point's Retreating Coast

[1] The ocean has always been a powerful force in human history. [2] This fall, our environmental science class spent nine weeks measuring the bluffs along Gannet Road. [3] We used survey stakes, old aerial photographs from the town library, and interviews with eleven residents. [4] What we found out and discovered in the end was that the bluff edge has moved back an average of about two feet every single year since 1990.

[5] The town's first answer to erosion was the concrete seawall built below Pell Street in 1998. [6] The wall protected the houses directly behind it for many years. [7] Anyone who still thinks walls are the answer simply has not looked at the beach. [8] Waves bouncing off the concrete have scoured away the sand in front of it, and the beach at Pell Street has nearly vanished.

[9] Dune restoration is a better way to protect the coast. [10] Last spring, volunteers planted beach grass and set sand fences along the north end of Little Cove. [11] Our stake measurements there showed that the bluff lost less than four inches this year, compared with two feet near the seawall. [12] The town has also moved the Gannet Road pump station 200 feet inland, and the lifeguard tower now sits on movable skids.

[13] Moving buildings is expensive. [14] Rebuilding them after a storm costs more. [15] Our class recommends that the council fund more dune planting and begin planning which structures should move first.

Testimony on Ordinance 14-B

[1] Good evening, members of the Larkhaven City Council. [2] My name is Odile Strand, and I have lived on Quarry Hill Road for twenty-two years. [3] Tonight I want to talk about lights.

[4] Every second Saturday, the Larkhaven Stargazers Club sets up telescopes in the gravel lot behind the public library. [5] Ten years ago, we could show visitors the faint smudge of the Andromeda galaxy without much trouble. [6] Since the city installed the new white LED globes along Cutler Avenue, that smudge has disappeared from our lot entirely. [7] Last spring a nine-year-old girl looked through my eyepiece, saw only a gray haze, and asked whether the telescope was broken.

[8] The problem is not that the lights are on but where they point. [9] The Cutler Avenue fixtures are uncovered globes that throw about a third of their light sideways and upward, where it lights nothing but the sky. [10] The town of Fenwick Ridge, forty miles north, replaced its globes with fully shielded fixtures and reported that its electricity bill for street lighting dropped by 18 percent. [11] Shielded fixtures, which aim light downward toward the street, they cost about the same as the globes the city currently uses and they also last just as long as the globes do.

[12] Anyway, that is basically all I have got, so thanks for listening to me ramble.

pub.passage:
ALTON original passage
What Your Phone Doesn't Know About Our Clay

[1] Every Saturday at the Hollins Lane Community Garden, someone asks why their tomatoes split, and every Saturday someone else answers by holding up a phone. [2] I am Ruth Okafor-Lind, I tend plot 14, and I want to make a case for a building most of us drive right past: the Pell Street Branch Library. [3] Libraries are good things to have in a town.

[4] A search engine gives you answers in a hurry, but it does not know our soil. [5] Our clay holds water for days, and advice written for sandy coastal gardens can drown a seedling here. [6] Pell Street keeps local knowledge that no search result can match. [7] Last spring I asked a librarian there, Mr. Dowd, about blossom-end rot, and he pulled out a county pamphlet from 1987 and a binder of notes left by a gardener who worked this same lot forty years ago.

[8] Search engines are completely useless for gardeners and should never be trusted. [9] Last year, the branch also began lending seeds from an old wooden card catalog near the front desk. [10] Gardeners borrow a packet in April, and in the fall they return seeds saved from their strongest plants. [11] The reason why this is important is because of the fact that the seeds that come back each year are seeds that have already proven that they can survive in our clay and our short summers.

[12] The county board votes on the library's budget on March 9. [13] Board members have proposed cutting the branch's Saturday hours, the only hours many working gardeners can visit, and the plan would close it's seed desk on weekends. [14] If you have ever borrowed a seed packet, a book, or a librarian's patience, come to the meeting and say so.

pub.passage:
ALTON original passage
What the Rock Teaches

¶1 On the first morning of the Keeper's School, the fog at Harrow Point was so thick that the eleven-year-olds could not see the lantern room from the landing, and one of them asked, reasonably, whether the lighthouse was still there. We climbed the hundred and twelve iron steps anyway. At the top, a girl named Pilar pressed her palm against the cold glass and announced that she could hear the shoal breaking even though she could not see it, and for the next ten minutes the whole class stood silent, listening to a hazard they had only ever read about. No worksheet I have ever written produced that silence.

¶2 I raise this scene because the Trust's board, at its spring meeting, asked a fair question: is a program that requires a ferry, a tide window, and a volunteer with a first-aid certificate really worth running when the same lessons could be taught in a heated room on the mainland? My answer, after one full year and fourteen visiting classes, is that the same lessons cannot be taught there, because at Harrow Point the building itself does most of the teaching. A lighthouse is not a backdrop for a curriculum; it is the curriculum.

¶3 Consider what the place demands before anyone opens a notebook. To arrive at all, students must read a tide table, because the landing floods two hours either side of high water. To climb, they must count their own breaths on the stairs and notice that the air grows colder as they rise. To understand why the lamp was built where it was, they must stand in the lantern room and look at the charted line of Castell Shoal, then look at the actual water and find the pale seam where the swell stumbles over rock. Every one of these tasks is a lesson in observation, and not one of them was designed by me. The keepers who logged the weather here for ninety years were, without knowing it, writing a textbook, and the children who copy their entries into fresh logbooks are not studying history so much as joining it.

¶4 I will not pretend the arrangement is convenient. The ferry costs the Trust roughly 340 dollars per crossing, three classes this year were cancelled by weather, and at least one student in every group is quietly, miserably seasick before we reach the dock. A thoughtful colleague on the mainland put the objection to me plainly: a good teacher can make a parking lot into a laboratory, so why spend the money on a rock? She is right that a good teacher can do a great deal. But the parking lot does not flood on schedule, does not rise a hundred feet into the wind, and does not keep a ninety-year record of its own weather. The teacher supplies the questions; the lighthouse supplies the consequences.

¶5 The consequences are what students remember. Of the 312 children who visited this year, 71 returned a follow-up postcard, and the ones we received did not mention the Fresnel lens or the vocabulary list. They mentioned the stairs, the fog, the moment the horn sounded, and the entry they wrote in the log. A boy from Saltmarsh Reach wrote that he now checks the tide before his family goes crabbing, which is, when you think about it, exactly what the lighthouse was built to make people do.

¶6 So I am asking the board to keep the ferry running, and I am asking members reading this column to say so at the autumn meeting. Harrow Point was decommissioned in 1994 because ships no longer needed it to find the shoal. It turns out that children still do.

ALTON original passage
What the Spreadsheet Cannot Hear

¶1 The memo arrived on a Tuesday, between a boiler quote and a reminder that my van inspection was overdue. The board, it said, is considering ending the ride-along program, which pairs first-year apprentices with a retired member for two days a month, and replacing it with a library of training videos. The videos, the memo assured us, would be professionally produced. I have no doubt that they would be. I also have no doubt that they would be a mistake, and I would like to explain why before the vote next month.

¶2 When I was nineteen I rode along with Augie Pell, who had been sweating copper since before I was born and who did not, as far as I could tell, approve of me. On my third day he stopped in a basement in Fenwick Heights, laid his palm against a supply line, and asked me what I heard. I heard nothing. He said that was the problem: the line was humming, faintly, and the hum meant a loose strap upstream that would, in a year or two, wear a hole through the pipe. He did not show me where the strap was; he made me stand there with my own hand on the pipe until I could feel what he felt, which took most of the afternoon and all of my pride.

¶3 There is a kind of knowledge that can be written down, and the trades are full of it: clearances, torque values, the order in which you open valves. A video carries that knowledge perfectly well. But there is another kind of knowledge that lives only in a person, and it is the kind that separates a plumber from someone who owns plumbing tools. It is the habit of noticing: the faint hum, the smell of flux mixed wrong, the way a homeowner's voice changes when the leak she describes is not the one she is worried about. No camera records a habit. A habit is transferred the way Augie transferred it, by standing next to someone long enough that his attention starts to shape yours.

¶4 I will grant the board its arithmetic. The program costs roughly 40,000 dollars a year, it reaches perhaps thirty apprentices, and some of our retired members are, to put it gently, set in their ways. A video library would cost less, reach everyone, and never tell an apprentice that her generation does not know how to work. But the expense that looks like waste on the spreadsheet is the whole point. What we are paying for is hours in basements, because time is the only medium in which attention passes from one pair of hands to another. Cut the hours and you have not made the program efficient; you have removed the thing it was for.

¶5 I should admit something the memo does not mention: the traffic on those ride-alongs does not run in one direction. Last spring I rode along myself, as the elder this time, with Teo Marsh, twenty-two, who carried a tablet the way I carry a pipe wrench. On our second job he pulled up a thermal image of a wall and found, in four minutes, a slab leak I had planned to hunt all morning with a listening rod. I was annoyed, and then I was grateful, and then I asked him to show me how the thing worked. He was patient with me, which is more than I can say for Augie. The retired members are not only being preserved by this program; they are being updated.

¶6 So here is what I am asking. Come to the meeting on the fourteenth, and when the board presents its cost per apprentice, ask whether the number counts the pipes that did not burst or the old plumbers who learned to read a thermal camera. You will not get an answer; nobody has one. That is not a flaw in the program. It is a description of what it does.
