pub.passage:
ALTON original passage

———

Source A
Four Towns Weigh One Library
Marisol Quent, The Valley Ledger, 2025

The Harlow Valley Council of Governments will vote in November on a plan to close the public library branches in Pennick, Oskar Bend, Lowen Mill and Dreyfield and replace them with a single regional hub on the former cannery lot in Pennick. The four branches together cost about 1.9 million dollars a year to run and recorded roughly 177,000 visits last year. Planners estimate the hub would cost 1.6 million dollars a year to operate and draw about 140,000 visits in its first full year, a figure they expect to climb once residents adjust. Construction is budgeted at 11 million dollars, with 4 million dollars coming from a state grant that lapses if the towns do not commit by spring. The hub would be open seven days and sixty-six hours a week; the current branches range from twenty hours a week in Dreyfield to forty-eight in Pennick. It would include a recording studio, a dedicated teen floor and a staffed homework center.

"We are not closing libraries, we are finally building one that can do what people keep asking us for," said council chair Ruthanne Bexley. Opponents point to distance. Dreyfield sits fourteen miles from the cannery lot, Lowen Mill nine and Oskar Bend six, and no public bus currently connects the four towns. Lowen Mill's representative, Tobias Enright, said he would not support the plan without "a written, funded answer for the people who walk to the library today." A council survey of 1,240 residents found that willingness to use the hub was highest in Pennick and fell steadily with distance.

———

Source B
Nostalgia Is Not a Library Budget
Desmond Kavale, retired branch director, The Harlow Valley Courier, 2025

I ran the Oskar Bend branch for nineteen years, and I loved it, so understand that I say this with no pleasure: the four-branch system is already a hub-and-nothing system. Pennick has the new books, the evening hours and the only children's librarian in the valley. The other three branches have what Pennick had eight years ago. When a Dreyfield teenager needs a quiet place to take an online exam, she borrows a car and drives to Pennick, because Dreyfield's building has two outlets and closes at four. We have been asking small towns to be loyal to buildings that cannot serve them.

Look at what it costs to open the doors. Every visit to Dreyfield costs the taxpayers 21.50 dollars; every visit to Pennick costs 7.50. That gap is not because Dreyfield's staff are careless. It is because a roof, a furnace, a security system and a desk clerk cost the same whether sixteen thousand people walk in or ninety-six thousand. Consolidating would free roughly 300,000 dollars a year, enough to hire three full-time specialists instead of four part-time generalists who rotate between buildings.

Yes, distance matters. But the honest comparison is not between a hub and four thriving branches. It is between a hub and four branches that are quietly rationing hours, materials and staff, and will ration more every year the furnaces age. A valley of eighteen thousand people can support one excellent library. It is proving, year by year, that it cannot support four adequate ones.

———

Source C
What Walks In at Three-Fifteen
Ilse Marrow, Dreyfield Town Newsletter, 2025

At three-fifteen the Dreyfield library fills the way a bus does. Eleven or twelve kids from the middle school come in with their backpacks half unzipped, and Mrs. Pell, who has worked the desk since before some of their parents were born, does not look up from her stamping until she has counted them. Then come the two retired men who read the paper on the bench by the window, and after them the woman from the apartments across the road who uses the one public computer to fill out her forms, because she has no computer and no car.

I have asked the council what these people are supposed to do on the day the doors close. I am told there may be a shuttle. A shuttle is a schedule, and a schedule is a reason not to go. A library you can walk to at three-fifteen is a different thing from a library you can be driven to on Saturdays.

The hub will be beautiful. I have seen the drawings, the teen floor and the recording studio, and I do not doubt that somebody in Pennick will use them. But the council survey put it plainly: only fourteen in a hundred Dreyfield residents expect to visit the hub as often as monthly. Thirty-three in a hundred visit our branch that often now. You cannot call that a service improvement. You can call it a service relocated to people who already have one. If the valley has 300,000 dollars a year to find, let it find it somewhere that does not take the only public room in this town.

———

Source D
Memorandum: Service Conditions for a Regional Library Hub
Office of Shared Services, Harlow Valley Council of Governments, 2025

This office was asked whether the proposed hub can be recommended as presented. Our answer is that it can be recommended only with three conditions attached, each funded in the same resolution that approves construction.

First, a fixed-route shuttle linking Dreyfield, Lowen Mill and Oskar Bend to the hub on at least four days a week, including one weekend day, at an estimated 95,000 dollars a year. Second, a staffed reading room of no fewer than twenty hours a week in Dreyfield and in Lowen Mill, housed in existing municipal buildings, with a public computer, holds pickup and a children's shelf, at an estimated 85,000 dollars a year for both. Third, a review after three years in which the hub's visit count is compared against the 140,000 projection, with the shuttle and reading rooms extended automatically if use from the outlying towns has not recovered to current levels.

These conditions reduce the projected annual saving from about 300,000 dollars to about 120,000 dollars. We consider that reduction the price of a plan that does not simply move service from the towns with the fewest alternatives to the town with the most. Without the conditions, the survey data suggest the hub would be used mainly by Pennick residents, and the valley would have spent 11 million dollars to serve roughly the people the Pennick branch already serves. With them, the hub becomes a genuine upgrade for every town rather than a consolidation that wears the name of one.

———

Source E (table)
Library Use and Expected Hub Use by Town
Harlow Valley Council of Governments resident survey, 2025

Results from the Harlow Valley Council of Governments resident survey of 1,240 adults, conducted by mail and online in the spring of 2025. Figures are the percentage of respondents in each town.

| Town | Visit a library branch at least monthly (percent) | Households with no car (percent) | Expect to visit the hub at least monthly (percent) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pennick | 41 | 9 | 44 |
| Oskar Bend | 38 | 12 | 31 |
| Lowen Mill | 35 | 15 | 22 |
| Dreyfield | 33 | 18 | 14 |
| All four towns | 38 | 12 | 34 |

———

Source F (chart)
Operating Cost per Visit, Current Branches and Proposed Hub
Finance Division, Harlow Valley Council of Governments, 2025

statements.prompt:
Many small towns share services such as fire protection, trash collection and school districts. Some are now asking whether public libraries should be shared the same way. In the fictional Harlow Valley, four towns are deciding whether to close their four small branch libraries and build one regional hub with longer hours, more staff and more equipment, located in the largest town. Supporters say one well-funded library serves everyone better than four underfunded ones. Opponents say a library people cannot walk to is not the same service in a new building.

Carefully read the six sources that follow, including the introductory information for each source. Then write an essay that synthesizes material from at least three of the sources and develops your position on whether a group of small towns should replace several small public libraries with one shared regional hub.

Your essay should:
- Respond to the prompt with a thesis that takes a defensible position on the question, which may be unconditional, conditional, or limited to particular circumstances.
- Select and use evidence from at least three of the provided sources to support your line of reasoning, and indicate clearly which sources you are using by citing them as Source A, Source B, and so on, or by the author's name.
- Explain how the evidence supports your reasoning; do not simply summarize or list what the sources say.
- You may use the sources to support, complicate, or argue against your own position, and you may draw on your own knowledge and experience in addition to the sources.

ALTON original passage
Who Was in the Room: Why Hollowmere Should Teach Chart Literacy

¶1 Last March, at a hearing of the Hollowmere County Council, a single chart nearly closed three branch libraries. The chart showed a line plunging from the upper left corner to the lower right, labeled Library Visits, 2019 to 2024, and several council members cited it in their remarks before the vote. The slide omitted one detail: its vertical axis began not at zero but at 410,000, so that a decline of about six percent looked, from the back of the room, like a collapse. The branches stayed open only because a retired surveyor in the audience asked to see the numbers behind the picture. This brief argues that the Hollowmere Unified School District should not leave such questions to the luck of who happens to be in the room.

¶2 We use the term chart literacy to mean the ability to read a data visualization as an argument rather than as a fact: to ask who drew it, what was left out, and what the chosen scale, color, and shape are doing to the viewer's judgment. It is not statistics, though it borrows from statistics, and it is not graphic design, though it borrows from that too. It is closer to the habit a careful reader brings to an editorial, the reflex of asking what the writer wants you to feel before you decide whether to feel it. Our recommendation is that this habit be taught deliberately, in a required unit for ninth and tenth graders, rather than assumed to arrive on its own.

¶3 The need is not speculative. In the spring of 2025, our office administered a short diagnostic to 1,140 students across four district high schools. Each student saw two bar charts describing the same fictional survey; one used a truncated axis and the other did not. Sixty-eight percent of students described the two charts as showing very different results, and fewer than one in five noticed the axis at all. When the same students were given five minutes of instruction on axis conventions and shown a third pair, the share who caught the truncation rose to just over half. Five minutes moved the needle; a semester, we believe, could move it much further.

¶4 Some members of the curriculum committee have reasonably asked whether this material belongs in an already crowded year, and whether it is really distinct from what mathematics teachers already cover. The concern about time is fair, and we do not propose adding a course; we propose a four-week unit that can live inside the existing civics or English sequence, where students are already learning to weigh sources. The concern about overlap is, we think, mistaken. Mathematics classes teach students to build charts correctly; almost no class teaches them what to do when someone else has built a chart incorrectly, or built it correctly and chosen the frame with care. The difference is the difference between learning to cook and learning to tell when a restaurant is hiding something under the sauce.

¶5 Consider how much of a citizen's year now arrives as a picture. Rent trends arrive as a line; crime arrives as a heat map; a candidate's record arrives as a pair of bars, one towering and one squat. These pictures are efficient, and we do not want students to distrust them wholesale, since a well-made chart can tell the truth faster than a paragraph can. But efficiency cuts both ways. A picture that persuades in two seconds also deceives in two seconds, and it leaves no sentence a reader can point to and call false.

¶6 The remainder of this brief sets out the proposed unit: four weeks of lessons, a cost of roughly 38 dollars per student, and the results of a pilot at Fenwick Ridge High School. We ask the board to read those sections with the surveyor in mind. He was not an expert; he simply knew which question to ask, and he was there. The district can make sure that, next time, a few hundred more people are.

ALTON original passage
Testimony on Ordinance 14-B

[1] Good evening, members of the Larkhaven City Council. [2] My name is Odile Strand, and I have lived on Quarry Hill Road for twenty-two years. [3] Tonight I want to talk about lights.

[4] Every second Saturday, the Larkhaven Stargazers Club sets up telescopes in the gravel lot behind the public library. [5] Ten years ago, we could show visitors the faint smudge of the Andromeda galaxy without much trouble. [6] Since the city installed the new white LED globes along Cutler Avenue, that smudge has disappeared from our lot entirely. [7] Last spring a nine-year-old girl looked through my eyepiece, saw only a gray haze, and asked whether the telescope was broken.

[8] The problem is not that the lights are on but where they point. [9] The Cutler Avenue fixtures are uncovered globes that throw about a third of their light sideways and upward, where it lights nothing but the sky. [10] The town of Fenwick Ridge, forty miles north, replaced its globes with fully shielded fixtures and reported that its electricity bill for street lighting dropped by 18 percent. [11] Shielded fixtures, which aim light downward toward the street, they cost about the same as the globes the city currently uses and they also last just as long as the globes do.

[12] Anyway, that is basically all I have got, so thanks for listening to me ramble.

ALTON original passage
The Gearhounds: A First-Season Report

[1] Last August, eleven students and one chemistry teacher met in the back corner of the woodshop at Harlow Creek High School with a donated toolbox, two secondhand motor kits, and no idea how to build a robot. [2] Eight months later, our robot, which we named Marmalade because of its orange zip ties, placed ninth out of twenty-six teams at the Tri-County Build Challenge in Dunmore. [3] This report is about what the Gearhounds did this year and some things that happened. [4] I am writing it because the Student Activities Board asked every new club for a summary before it votes on next year's budgets.

[5] The team spent September and October learning basics: how to wire a motor controller, how to read a gear ratio, how to keep a chassis from twisting. [6] Our first drive base, finished in November, could not turn left. [7] Instead of starting over, we traced the problem to a mismatched pair of wheels and swapped them in a single afternoon. [8] By February, Marmalade could lift a foam block, drive over a ramp, and park itself inside a taped square, the three tasks the competition required. [9] Honestly, the judges were kind of blown away that a first-year team even showed up with a working bot.

[10] The members learned a great deal from the season. [11] Several of the students who joined had never used a power drill before, by March they were teaching the eighth graders who visited on shadow day. [12] Our faculty adviser, Ms. Delacroix-Tam, kept a sign-in sheet, and attendance never dropped below nine members, even during exam week.

[13] Next year the team needs a locking storage cabinet, a second set of batteries, and roughly 900 dollars for competition registration. [14] The board should fund us because robotics is obviously the coolest club at the school and everyone knows it. [15] We are not asking for a new room or a new teacher; we are asking for a shelf, a charger, and a chance to finish what we started.

pub.passage:
ALTON original passage
Who Wrote the English Sentences

¶1 Last Tuesday the Ambervale Prize announced its shortlist, and the press release named six novels, six authors, and six publishers, but not one translator. Four of those six books were written in languages the jury does not read. I know this because I translated one of them. My name appears on page four of the paperback, in a typeface smaller than the one used to describe the paper stock.

¶2 Readers sometimes imagine translation as a kind of plumbing: the words flow in one end of the pipe in Norwegian and come out the other end in English, and the translator merely checks for leaks. The image is comforting, and it is wrong. A sentence in one language is not a container with a fixed amount of meaning inside it; it is a set of choices that a second language cannot reproduce but can only answer. When the Norwegian novelist Sigrun Aalvik wrote that her heroine "went out into the weather," she used a verb that in her dialect also means to quarrel. English has no such verb. I had to decide whether the woman walked into a storm or into an argument, and whichever I chose, the English reader would believe the author had chosen it.

¶3 Consider the scale of the problem. Aalvik's novel runs to roughly ninety thousand words, and I made, by my own rough count, something near forty decisions a page that no dictionary could make for me: where to break a sentence, which of three possible synonyms carried the right chill, whether a joke survived or had to be replaced with a different joke. Multiply that by three hundred pages and you arrive at an English book that shares a plot and a spirit with the Norwegian one but shares none of its sentences. Every sentence the English reader admires, I wrote. Every sentence the reader finds clumsy, I also wrote.

¶4 I can hear the objection, because I have made it myself at dinner parties: the story, the characters, the architecture of the book belong to Aalvik, and the translator is at most a skilled carpenter working from her drawings. There is something to this. I did not invent the heroine, and I would not want credit for her. But a carpenter who selects every board, every joint, and every finish, and whose work the client lives inside for years, is not usually left off the plaque. Architecture is credited; so is the building.

¶5 Why, then, does the convention of the invisible translator persist? Partly because publishers fear that a second name on the cover warns the buyer that the book is foreign, and foreign, in the sales meeting, means difficult. Partly because reviewers, who seldom read the original, find it easier to praise "the author's luminous prose" than to admit they are praising prose whose author they cannot identify. And partly, I confess, because translators themselves have cultivated a monkish modesty, as though visibility were a kind of vanity. The effect is circular: because we are unnamed, we seem unimportant, and because we seem unimportant, nobody thinks to name us.

¶6 I am not asking for the author's name to be removed, or shrunk, or shared with mine in some awkward hyphenated compound. I am asking for a line of type on the front of the book, the same size as the blurb from a novelist nobody has heard of, that says who wrote the English sentences. If you run a prize, name the translator in the press release. If you review books, say which words you are actually quoting. And if you are a reader who has ever loved a novel written in a language you do not speak, you have already loved a translator's work; you simply were not told whom to thank.

Most of the fighting about car-free downtowns assumes there are only two choices: close the street or leave it alone. Marisol Teague's column about Carrow Street shows why that framing doesn't work. The hardware store owner, the baker, and the nurse are not just three opinions about cars. They are three different kinds of trips. A city should limit private cars downtown only on the blocks and during the hours when people come to stay, and it should keep car access wherever people come to fetch something heavy or have to leave after dark. How much a city restricts cars should depend on why people are on the street, not on one rule for all six blocks.

Start with the hardware store and the bakery, since they seem like opposites. The baker's customers come to linger. They buy a roll, sit down, maybe buy another, and Teague says people linger "when nothing is idling at their backs." For them the closed street is the product. The hardware customer is on an errand. Nobody lingers with a stack of two-by-fours, and nobody carries them eight blocks to a garage. So the closure costs the hardware store exactly the thing it sells, which is convenience. The fix is not to reopen the whole street. The city could put short loading bays at each end of the closed blocks, or let pickup trucks in before 9 a.m. on Saturdays. I'll admit this might not save every lumber sale. If the store is in the middle of the six blocks, a bay at the corner is still a long haul. In that case the honest answer is that some businesses don't fit a pedestrian block, and the city should either leave that one block open to slow traffic or help the store pay for delivery. Pretending the bakery's success makes up for the hardware store's loss is how the city ended up with a quarrel instead of a plan.

The nurse looks like the same complaint, but it isn't. Her problem has nothing to do with carrying anything. It's about time and safety. At eleven at night the bakery is closed and nobody is lingering, so the reason for closing the street is gone, but the closure is still pushing her eight blocks from her car. This is the easiest case to solve, because lingering happens at predictable hours. In my town, Main Street closes for the farmers market on Saturday mornings, and by one o'clock the barricades are gone and cars are parked at the curb again. Nobody fights about it, because the closure lines up with when people actually want to walk around. Carrow Street could do the same and reopen to cars at nine every night. Then the nurse isn't trading her safety for someone else's croissant.

Getting the degree wrong has consequences that reach past downtown. Teague mentions that the hardware customers now drive to "the outlet strip on the highway." If a city closes too much, it doesn't get rid of cars. It moves them, and it sorts people. Downtown ends up for people with free time and good legs, and everyone running errands, working night shifts, or unable to walk far gets sent to the highway. That's also why the right amount of restriction should change from city to city. A city with buses running late can close more, because the nurse has another way home. A small city like Verrick Falls, where the car is the only option for a lot of people, has to close less, and it has to close more carefully.

Teague says a downtown must be a place people can reach and a place people want to stay. Those two purposes don't really have to compete if the city stops treating the street as one thing.    - "How much a city restricts cars should depend on why people are on the street, not on one rule for all six blocks." - This states the principle the body paragraphs will use, so it sets up a line of reasoning and doesn't just repeat the prompt.
   - "So the closure costs the hardware store exactly the thing it sells, which is convenience." - This is commentary, not summary. It explains why an errand business is hurt by a closure when a lingering business is helped, which ties the evidence to how much of the street to close.
   - "I'll admit this might not save every lumber sale.    - "At eleven at night the bakery is closed and nobody is lingering, so the reason for closing the street is gone" - The nurse's situation is treated as a problem the position has to solve, and the writer applies their own reasoning to solve it. It's about time and safety." - The essay uses Teague's three people as a test for one principle and argues that the nurse and the hardware customer are different problems with different solutions. Sample response, middle score (4/6; Thesis 1, Evidence and commentary 3, Sophistication 0):
A city should limit private cars downtown only part of the time and only on the blocks where people mostly come to browse and eat, while keeping curbside access on the blocks where people come to carry things away. In other words, how much a city limits cars should depend on what each street is used for, not on one rule for the whole downtown.

The column about Verrick Falls shows why one rule does not work. The hardware store owner lost his Saturday customers because they used to park at the curb and load lumber, and now they drive to the outlet strip on the highway. You cannot carry lumber several blocks from a parking garage. This shows that a store that sells heavy things depends on cars, and if the city closes the street in front of it, the store loses business to the highway. The bakery owner has the opposite experience, since she sells more rolls when people can linger with nothing idling behind them. Bakeries and cafes sell a pleasant stop, so a quiet street helps them. So the closing of Carrow Street helped one business and hurt another, which means a city should look at what businesses are on a street before it closes it.

I have seen something like this in my own town. The street near my school with the coffee shops and the used bookstore has a farmers market on Sundays with the road blocked off, and it is always crowded and people seem happy. But the same weekend nobody would want the pharmacy two streets over to be blocked off, because older people drive there to pick up prescriptions and they cannot walk far. A closing that works for a market would not work for a pharmacy.

The nurse in the column is a harder problem. She gets off at eleven at night and has to walk eight blocks to the garage. I think the answer is time of day. The street can be closed during the day and on weekends when it is busy, and opened to cars at night so she can park close and feel safe. This costs the city something, because the street is less of a park at night, but there are few people lingering at that hour anyway, so the loss is small. Nobody is hurt much by letting cars back in at night, while the nurse could be hurt a lot.

Some people will say that any cars at all ruin a walkable downtown. But a downtown that nobody can reach is not walkable either, it is just empty. The best position is a middle one, with closures on the blocks and hours when lingering matters most, and cars allowed where people have to reach something. That way the city gets both purposes the column names, a place people can reach and a place they want to stay.

Earns the thesis point.
   - "You cannot carry lumber several blocks from a parking garage." - Uses the hardware store from the column and gives a real mechanism (heavy goods need curb access), and the point is stated rather than developed.
   - "So the closing of Carrow Street helped one business and hurt another, which means a city should look at what businesses are on a street before it closes it." - Links the two column examples back to the thesis, giving a followable line of reasoning, though the point is fairly general.
   - "A closing that works for a market would not work for a pharmacy." - Personal example is specific enough to count, but the pharmacy is described briefly and the commentary is thin and repeats the earlier point about different businesses.
   - "I think the answer is time of day." - Treats the nurse as a problem the position must solve, which is good, but the solution is stated simply and the claim that few people linger at night is asserted without support.
   - "But a downtown that nobody can reach is not walkable either, it is just empty." - Brief rebuttal of the opposing view; it is a single sentence and the essay does not explore unintended consequences, so no sustained sophistication.

Sample response, low score (1/6; Thesis 0, Evidence and commentary 1, Sophistication 0):
Cities have to decide how much to limit cars downtown and there are good points on both sides. In my opinion a city should limit cars but not too much, because downtowns need both cars and people walking.

In the column, Verrick Falls closed six blocks of Carrow Street and now people are arguing. The hardware store owner says his customers go to the highway now. The bakery lady says she sells more rolls. And the nurse is worried about walking to the garage at night. This shows that the issue is complicated because different people want different things. Some businesses like the closing and some do not.

I think that closing streets is good because people like to walk around. When there are no cars it is quieter and cleaner and people stay longer. Also it is safer for kids. A lot of cities have done this and it works for them. Studies show that walkable downtowns do better, so cities should do it more.

However, cars are important too. Not everybody can walk far, like old people or people who work late. If a city closes everything then people will just go somewhere else, like the outlet strip. That would hurt downtown. So a city should not close all of it.

In conclusion, a city should close some streets but leave some open for cars. This way the bakery and the hardware store can both be happy and the nurse can get to her car. It is a balance and each city has to find the right amount for them.
   - "a city should limit cars but not too much, because downtowns need both cars and people walking" - Takes a position, but 'not too much' is vague and the essay never says what the limit should depend on or where the line falls. This is close to restating the prompt's tension, so the thesis point is likely not earned.
   - "Cities have to decide how much to limit cars downtown and there are good points on both sides." - Restates the prompt almost word for word and gestures at 'both sides' without committing to anything arguable.
   - "This shows that the issue is complicated because different people want different things." - Summarizes the hardware owner, baker and nurse and concludes it is 'complicated' with no argument built from them. This is the level-1 pattern of listing the three figures.
   - "Studies show that walkable downtowns do better, so cities should do it more." - Generic appeal to unnamed studies, with no specific example or explanation of the mechanism. This is the kind of generality that caps evidence at 1.
   - "A lot of cities have done this and it works for them." - No city is named and no scene is described, so this is assertion rather than evidence. Commentary is absent.
   - "This way the bakery and the hardware store can both be happy and the nurse can get to her car." - Proposes a compromise but never explains how leaving some streets open would serve each purpose, or why the hardware customer and the nurse are different problems. The compromise is not tested against the tension Teague names, so there is no sophistication.
   - "It is a balance and each city has to find the right amount for them." - Falls back on 'it's a balance' and leaves the tension unresolved. This gestures at complexity without working through it.

   - "So the closing of Carrow Street helped one business and hurt another, which means a city should look at what businesses are on a street before it closes it." - Links the two column examples back to the thesis, giving a followable line of reasoning, though the point is fairly general.
   - "A closing that works for a market would not work for a pharmacy." - Personal example is specific enough to count, but the pharmacy is described briefly and the commentary is thin and repeats the earlier point about different businesses.
   - "I think the answer is time of day." - Treats the nurse as a problem the position must solve, which is good, but the solution is stated simply and the claim that few people linger at night is asserted without support.
   - "But a downtown that nobody can reach is not walkable either, it is just empty." - Brief rebuttal of the opposing view; it is a single sentence and the essay does not explore unintended consequences, so no sustained sophistication.

Sample response, low score (1/6; Thesis 0, Evidence and commentary 1, Sophistication 0):
Cities have to decide how much to limit cars downtown and there are good points on both sides. In my opinion a city should limit cars but not too much, because downtowns need both cars and people walking.

In the column, Verrick Falls closed six blocks of Carrow Street and now people are arguing. The hardware store owner says his customers go to the highway now. The bakery lady says she sells more rolls. And the nurse is worried about walking to the garage at night. This shows that the issue is complicated because different people want different things. Some businesses like the closing and some do not.

I think that closing streets is good because people like to walk around. When there are no cars it is quieter and cleaner and people stay longer. Also it is safer for kids. A lot of cities have done this and it works for them. Studies show that walkable downtowns do better, so cities should do it more.

However, cars are important too. Not everybody can walk far, like old people or people who work late. If a city closes everything then people will just go somewhere else, like the outlet strip. That would hurt downtown. So a city should not close all of it.

In conclusion, a city should close some streets but leave some open for cars. This way the bakery and the hardware store can both be happy and the nurse can get to her car. It is a balance and each city has to find the right amount for them.
   - "a city should limit cars but not too much, because downtowns need both cars and people walking" - Takes a position, but 'not too much' is vague and the essay never says what the limit should depend on or where the line falls. This is close to restating the prompt's tension, so the thesis point is likely not earned.
   - "Cities have to decide how much to limit cars downtown and there are good points on both sides." - Restates the prompt almost word for word and gestures at 'both sides' without committing to anything arguable.
   - "This shows that the issue is complicated because different people want different things." - Summarizes the hardware owner, baker and nurse and concludes it is 'complicated' with no argument built from them. This is the level-1 pattern of listing the three figures.
   - "Studies show that walkable downtowns do better, so cities should do it more." - Generic appeal to unnamed studies, with no specific example or explanation of the mechanism. This is the kind of generality that caps evidence at 1.
   - "A lot of cities have done this and it works for them." - No city is named and no scene is described, so this is assertion rather than evidence. Commentary is absent.
   - "This way the bakery and the hardware store can both be happy and the nurse can get to her car." - Proposes a compromise but never explains how leaving some streets open would serve each purpose, or why the hardware customer and the nurse are different problems. The compromise is not tested against the tension Teague names, so there is no sophistication.
   - "It is a balance and each city has to find the right amount for them." - Falls back on 'it's a balance' and leaves the tension unresolved. This gestures at complexity without working through it.

The Gearhounds: A First-Season Report

[1] Last August, eleven students and one chemistry teacher met in the back corner of the woodshop at Harlow Creek High School with a donated toolbox, two secondhand motor kits, and no idea how to build a robot. [2] Eight months later, our robot, which we named Marmalade because of its orange zip ties, placed ninth out of twenty-six teams at the Tri-County Build Challenge in Dunmore. [3] This report is about what the Gearhounds did this year and some things that happened. [4] I am writing it because the Student Activities Board asked every new club for a summary before it votes on next year's budgets.

[5] The team spent September and October learning basics: how to wire a motor controller, how to read a gear ratio, how to keep a chassis from twisting. [6] Our first drive base, finished in November, could not turn left. [7] Instead of starting over, we traced the problem to a mismatched pair of wheels and swapped them in a single afternoon. [8] By February, Marmalade could lift a foam block, drive over a ramp, and park itself inside a taped square, the three tasks the competition required. [9] Honestly, the judges were kind of blown away that a first-year team even showed up with a working bot.

[10] The members learned a great deal from the season. [11] Several of the students who joined had never used a power drill before, by March they were teaching the eighth graders who visited on shadow day. [12] Our faculty adviser, Ms. Delacroix-Tam, kept a sign-in sheet, and attendance never dropped below nine members, even during exam week.

[13] Next year the team needs a locking storage cabinet, a second set of batteries, and roughly 900 dollars for competition registration. [14] The board should fund us because robotics is obviously the coolest club at the school and everyone knows it. [15] We are not asking for a new room or a new teacher; we are asking for a shelf, a charger, and a chance to finish what we started.

pub.passage:
ALTON original passage
Who Was in the Room: Why Hollowmere Should Teach Chart Literacy

¶1 Last March, at a hearing of the Hollowmere County Council, a single chart nearly closed three branch libraries. The chart showed a line plunging from the upper left corner to the lower right, labeled Library Visits, 2019 to 2024, and several council members cited it in their remarks before the vote. The slide omitted one detail: its vertical axis began not at zero but at 410,000, so that a decline of about six percent looked, from the back of the room, like a collapse. The branches stayed open only because a retired surveyor in the audience asked to see the numbers behind the picture. This brief argues that the Hollowmere Unified School District should not leave such questions to the luck of who happens to be in the room.

¶2 We use the term chart literacy to mean the ability to read a data visualization as an argument rather than as a fact: to ask who drew it, what was left out, and what the chosen scale, color, and shape are doing to the viewer's judgment. It is not statistics, though it borrows from statistics, and it is not graphic design, though it borrows from that too. It is closer to the habit a careful reader brings to an editorial, the reflex of asking what the writer wants you to feel before you decide whether to feel it. Our recommendation is that this habit be taught deliberately, in a required unit for ninth and tenth graders, rather than assumed to arrive on its own.

¶3 The need is not speculative. In the spring of 2025, our office administered a short diagnostic to 1,140 students across four district high schools. Each student saw two bar charts describing the same fictional survey; one used a truncated axis and the other did not. Sixty-eight percent of students described the two charts as showing very different results, and fewer than one in five noticed the axis at all. When the same students were given five minutes of instruction on axis conventions and shown a third pair, the share who caught the truncation rose to just over half. Five minutes moved the needle; a semester, we believe, could move it much further.

¶4 Some members of the curriculum committee have reasonably asked whether this material belongs in an already crowded year, and whether it is really distinct from what mathematics teachers already cover. The concern about time is fair, and we do not propose adding a course; we propose a four-week unit that can live inside the existing civics or English sequence, where students are already learning to weigh sources. The concern about overlap is, we think, mistaken. Mathematics classes teach students to build charts correctly; almost no class teaches them what to do when someone else has built a chart incorrectly, or built it correctly and chosen the frame with care. The difference is the difference between learning to cook and learning to tell when a restaurant is hiding something under the sauce.

¶5 Consider how much of a citizen's year now arrives as a picture. Rent trends arrive as a line; crime arrives as a heat map; a candidate's record arrives as a pair of bars, one towering and one squat. These pictures are efficient, and we do not want students to distrust them wholesale, since a well-made chart can tell the truth faster than a paragraph can. But efficiency cuts both ways. A picture that persuades in two seconds also deceives in two seconds, and it leaves no sentence a reader can point to and call false.

¶6 The remainder of this brief sets out the proposed unit: four weeks of lessons, a cost of roughly 38 dollars per student, and the results of a pilot at Fenwick Ridge High School. We ask the board to read those sections with the surveyor in mind. He was not an expert; he simply knew which question to ask, and he was there. The district can make sure that, next time, a few hundred more people are.

pub.passage:
ALTON original passage
The Widow's Ledger

¶1 On a Tuesday evening in March, the Halverton City Council spent forty minutes debating whether a schoolteacher named Priya Castellanos could keep two hives on the roof of her garage. I sat in the back row with a folder of photocopies from the municipal archive, where I have worked for eleven years, and listened to a councilman warn that bees "do not belong in a modern city." He said it as if the matter were settled, as if modern and bee were words that had never shared a sentence. They have shared a great many, and most of them were written in Halverton.

¶2 The first beekeeper in our records was not a farmer but a tanner's widow, Agnes Durrow, who in 1891 set four straw skeps against the brick wall behind her rowhouse on Cordage Street. Her ledger survives, and it is a modest, stubborn document: so many pounds of honey sold to the druggist, so many to the bakery, a jar given to the priest, a sting noted and then forgotten. By 1905 the city directory listed nineteen households that kept bees, and the honey they produced was dark and faintly mineral, flavored by the linden trees the city had planted along the trolley lines. The bees, in other words, did not merely tolerate the city; they ate it, and gave something back.

¶3 Then came 1923. A boy on Fulling Lane was stung several times after poking a hive with a broom handle, and the Halverton Evening Courier ran the story under a headline that called the bees "a swarm of menace." Within a month the council passed an ordinance forbidding hives within the city limits, and within a year the nineteen households had become none. Nothing had changed about the bees. What had changed was the story the city told about itself: it was becoming a place of paved streets and electric signs, and a straw skep behind a rowhouse looked, suddenly, like a thing left over from a slower century. The ban was less a response to danger than a tidying away of the past.

¶4 I do not want to pretend the worries were all invented. Bees sting, and a hive placed on a fire escape above a crowded sidewalk is a poor neighbor; the boy on Fulling Lane spent two days in bed, and his mother's anger was neither foolish nor small. But a city that outlawed every creature capable of causing two days in bed would have to begin with its horses, its trolleys, and its own citizens. The question was never whether bees could do harm. The question was whether the harm was large enough to justify erasing a practice that fed bakeries, pollinated gardens, and gave a tanner's widow a trade of her own.

¶5 The practice did not stay erased. In 1974 a retired machinist named Oscar Lindqvist quietly installed a hive on the roof of a shuttered hat factory, and the inspectors who discovered it three summers later could not bring themselves to write him up. The ordinance was repealed in 1981, and the hives came back the way weeds come back to a vacant lot, first in one place, then in a dozen, then everywhere the sun reached. Today the archive holds photographs of hives on the library roof, in the courtyard of the firehouse, and behind the same rowhouse on Cordage Street where Agnes Durrow kept hers.

¶6 So when the councilman says bees do not belong in a modern city, I want to hand him the ledger. Bees have belonged to Halverton for longer than its sewers, its streetlights, or its council chamber. What they ask of us is small: a roof, a water dish, a measure of patience with the occasional sting. What they offer in return is a reminder that a city is not only pavement and ordinance but a living thing, and that the people who tend small, stubborn, useful work in its corners are not relics of a slower century. They are the ones who keep it alive.
