pub.passage:
ALTON original passage
Who Else Will Come: On Conrad Weil's Siren on the Ridge

¶1 The pager goes off at ten past two in the morning, and for eleven years my first thought was never about the fire but about who else would come. In Brannock County, where I served with the Marrow Creek Volunteer Fire Company until my knees retired me, a structure fire draws whoever is awake, sober, and within fifteen miles. Some nights that is nine people; some nights it is three. Conrad Weil's new book, Siren on the Ridge, is the first account I have read that understands this arithmetic, and it deserves a wide readership among the county commissioners who will decide, over the next decade, whether rural counties keep a volunteer fire service at all.

¶2 Weil's reporting is the book's great strength. He spent two years riding with departments in six counties across three states, and he lets the volunteers speak in their own flat, unsentimental voices. The numbers he gathers are grim: at one station the average age of a responder rose from thirty-four to fifty-seven in twenty years, and the roster shrank from twenty-two names to nine. He describes a chief who answers calls alone because there is no one else, and a township that dissolved its company and now waits forty minutes for an engine from the next county. These are not isolated anecdotes; they are the shape of the thing.

¶3 Where the book falters is in its diagnosis. Weil concludes that the volunteer model is simply obsolete, a relic of a time when men worked within walking distance of the station and could leave the mill when the whistle blew, and he argues that counties should accept the inevitable and hire paid crews. I grant that the old pattern is gone; nobody leaves a shift at a distribution warehouse forty miles away to answer a brush fire. But obsolete is the wrong word for a system that has been quietly loaded with burdens it was never designed to carry. The state now requires one hundred eighty hours of certified training before a recruit may enter a burning building, up from forty when I joined. The company must also buy its own equipment, which means that the same nine people who fight the fires also run the fish fry, the raffle, the mailer, and the pancake breakfast that pays for the air packs. We did not lose volunteers because people stopped caring about their neighbors. We lost them because we asked each one to be a firefighter, a fundraiser, a mechanic, and a grant writer, and then wondered why only retirees had the hours.

¶4 Asking a fire company to sell raffle tickets for its own breathing apparatus is like asking a lifeguard to run a lemonade stand to pay for the pool. The absurdity would be obvious anywhere else. Yet Weil treats the fundraising burden as a charming folkway rather than the structural failure it is, and so he never asks the question that matters: what happens to the roster when the county, not the fish fry, buys the truck?

¶5 We have some evidence, and it is more hopeful than Weil allows. Tillery County, two hours north of us, passed a modest fire levy six years ago, roughly the price of a tank of gas per household per year, and used it to cover equipment and to reimburse recruits for their training hours. Its volunteer roster has grown by a third since, and the average age of a new recruit is twenty-nine. The people were there all along. They had simply been priced out of serving.

¶6 So read Siren on the Ridge for its portraits, which are honest and often moving, and for its warning, which is overdue. But read it skeptically when it reaches for the obituary. Volunteer fire service is not dying of old age; it is being starved, and starvation, unlike age, has a remedy. If you sit on a county board, the remedy is in your budget. The pager will go off tonight somewhere in your district, and the only question that matters is who else will come.

pub.passage:
ALTON original passage
The Gearhounds: A First-Season Report

[1] Last August, eleven students and one chemistry teacher met in the back corner of the woodshop at Harlow Creek High School with a donated toolbox, two secondhand motor kits, and no idea how to build a robot. [2] Eight months later, our robot, which we named Marmalade because of its orange zip ties, placed ninth out of twenty-six teams at the Tri-County Build Challenge in Dunmore. [3] This report is about what the Gearhounds did this year and some things that happened. [4] I am writing it because the Student Activities Board asked every new club for a summary before it votes on next year's budgets.

[5] The team spent September and October learning basics: how to wire a motor controller, how to read a gear ratio, how to keep a chassis from twisting. [6] Our first drive base, finished in November, could not turn left. [7] Instead of starting over, we traced the problem to a mismatched pair of wheels and swapped them in a single afternoon. [8] By February, Marmalade could lift a foam block, drive over a ramp, and park itself inside a taped square, the three tasks the competition required. [9] Honestly, the judges were kind of blown away that a first-year team even showed up with a working bot.

[10] The members learned a great deal from the season. [11] Several of the students who joined had never used a power drill before, by March they were teaching the eighth graders who visited on shadow day. [12] Our faculty adviser, Ms. Delacroix-Tam, kept a sign-in sheet, and attendance never dropped below nine members, even during exam week.

[13] Next year the team needs a locking storage cabinet, a second set of batteries, and roughly 900 dollars for competition registration. [14] The board should fund us because robotics is obviously the coolest club at the school and everyone knows it. [15] We are not asking for a new room or a new teacher; we are asking for a shelf, a charger, and a chance to finish what we started.

pub.passage:
ALTON original passage
Who Was in the Room: Why Hollowmere Should Teach Chart Literacy

¶1 Last March, at a hearing of the Hollowmere County Council, a single chart nearly closed three branch libraries. The chart showed a line plunging from the upper left corner to the lower right, labeled Library Visits, 2019 to 2024, and several council members cited it in their remarks before the vote. The slide omitted one detail: its vertical axis began not at zero but at 410,000, so that a decline of about six percent looked, from the back of the room, like a collapse. The branches stayed open only because a retired surveyor in the audience asked to see the numbers behind the picture. This brief argues that the Hollowmere Unified School District should not leave such questions to the luck of who happens to be in the room.

¶2 We use the term chart literacy to mean the ability to read a data visualization as an argument rather than as a fact: to ask who drew it, what was left out, and what the chosen scale, color, and shape are doing to the viewer's judgment. It is not statistics, though it borrows from statistics, and it is not graphic design, though it borrows from that too. It is closer to the habit a careful reader brings to an editorial, the reflex of asking what the writer wants you to feel before you decide whether to feel it. Our recommendation is that this habit be taught deliberately, in a required unit for ninth and tenth graders, rather than assumed to arrive on its own.

¶3 The need is not speculative. In the spring of 2025, our office administered a short diagnostic to 1,140 students across four district high schools. Each student saw two bar charts describing the same fictional survey; one used a truncated axis and the other did not. Sixty-eight percent of students described the two charts as showing very different results, and fewer than one in five noticed the axis at all. When the same students were given five minutes of instruction on axis conventions and shown a third pair, the share who caught the truncation rose to just over half. Five minutes moved the needle; a semester, we believe, could move it much further.

¶4 Some members of the curriculum committee have reasonably asked whether this material belongs in an already crowded year, and whether it is really distinct from what mathematics teachers already cover. The concern about time is fair, and we do not propose adding a course; we propose a four-week unit that can live inside the existing civics or English sequence, where students are already learning to weigh sources. The concern about overlap is, we think, mistaken. Mathematics classes teach students to build charts correctly; almost no class teaches them what to do when someone else has built a chart incorrectly, or built it correctly and chosen the frame with care. The difference is the difference between learning to cook and learning to tell when a restaurant is hiding something under the sauce.

¶5 Consider how much of a citizen's year now arrives as a picture. Rent trends arrive as a line; crime arrives as a heat map; a candidate's record arrives as a pair of bars, one towering and one squat. These pictures are efficient, and we do not want students to distrust them wholesale, since a well-made chart can tell the truth faster than a paragraph can. But efficiency cuts both ways. A picture that persuades in two seconds also deceives in two seconds, and it leaves no sentence a reader can point to and call false.

¶6 The remainder of this brief sets out the proposed unit: four weeks of lessons, a cost of roughly 38 dollars per student, and the results of a pilot at Fenwick Ridge High School. We ask the board to read those sections with the surveyor in mind. He was not an expert; he simply knew which question to ask, and he was there. The district can make sure that, next time, a few hundred more people are.

pub.passage:
ALTON original passage
Sixty-One Sycamores

¶1 When I was twenty-three and newly hired by the town of Harrow Fen, my supervisor handed me a clipboard and told me to count the trees on Calder Avenue. I assumed it was busywork. It took four days, because every sycamore on that street had something to say: a hollow where a raccoon had raised three litters, a lightning scar healed over like a closed eye, a root that had lifted a sidewalk slab and then, with a patience I did not yet understand, grown around it. Graduates, I have been asked to speak to you about your futures, and I intend to, but I am going to do it by talking about those sycamores, because last Tuesday the council voted to widen Calder Avenue, and the plan calls for removing all sixty-one of them.

¶2 Let me be precise about what we mean when we say old-growth on a city street, since the phrase was borrowed from forestry and does not fit perfectly. In a forest, old growth describes a stand that has never been cleared. On a street, it describes something rarer: a tree that has survived a century of paving, trenching, salt, and committees. Every one of those sycamores was planted by a person who knew they would never sit in its shade. That is not sentiment; that is the definition.

¶3 You have spent years learning to call things by their proper names, so call a street tree what it is: infrastructure. A storm sewer carries water away; a mature sycamore intercepts roughly three thousand gallons of rainfall a year before it ever reaches the sewer. A transformer cools a block in August; the canopy on Calder lowers surface temperature by double digits, according to the thermal survey our own department commissioned seven years ago. We do not demolish a bridge because it is old. We inspect it, we repair it, and when we must, we close a lane. Yet the same council that budgets forty years of maintenance for a culvert will vote to erase a hundred and forty years of canopy in an afternoon, because a tree, unlike a culvert, does not appear on the balance sheet as an asset that depreciates.

¶4 I will concede the obvious. Some old trees must come down. I have signed the removal orders myself, standing under a red oak with a fungal rot that had eaten two-thirds of its heartwood, and I did not sleep well afterward, but I signed. A dangerous tree is not a monument; it is a liability with leaves. But the Calder sycamores are not dangerous. The widening is proposed so that traffic can move eleven seconds faster at the Pell Street light. Eleven seconds. We are being asked to trade a century for a fraction of a minute, and to call the trade progress.

¶5 So here is what I am asking of you, and it is harder than it sounds. You will be the ones in the room when the next Calder Avenue comes up for a vote. You will have the drawings, the models, the cost estimates, and you will be tempted to treat a mature tree the way the software treats it: as a circle on a plan, easily erased and easily redrawn somewhere else. Resist that. A sapling planted in mitigation is not a replacement; it is an IOU that will not be paid during your career, or your children's. Insist that the removal of an old-growth street tree be justified the way we justify closing a hospital wing: reluctantly, publicly, and with the arithmetic on the table.

¶6 I counted sixty-one sycamores in my first week of work. I would like to count them again at the end of yours. Go and be the kind of planners who make that possible.

The central bank guarantees every loan and makes the payments. is incorrect: Banks, not the central bank, make the loans.
Banks keep all deposits as reserves and charge fees to depositors. is incorrect: A fractional reserve system lends part of deposits.
Banks print currency whenever customers ask for loans. is incorrect: Banks create deposits, not currency; the central bank issues currency.
Banks lend out the required reserves in addition to excess reserves. is incorrect: Required reserves must be held, not lent.

Scoring guide (ALTON practice rubric, not official College Board scoring). Each essay is worth 6 points.
Thesis (0-1): Positions that count as defensible: any claim about whether, how much, or under what conditions a craft requirement is justified, including claims that reframe the question (for instance, that what matters is not craft but any activity with irreversible consequences). A thesis that argues only about automation in general, with no connection to a school requirement, does not answer this prompt.
   - 1: The essay states a defensible claim about how far schools should require a hand craft, which may be a full endorsement, a full rejection, or a qualified position (for example: required only in early grades, required but counted toward existing elective time, optional but strongly incentivized, required only if taught as problem-solving rather than vocational training). The thesis may appear anywhere in the essay and may be more than one sentence, but it must commit to a stance a reader could disagree with.
   - 0: No thesis, or a thesis that only restates the prompt (for example, 'There are many opinions about whether schools should require crafts'), or a thesis that states a position without taking any side on the requirement question (for example, 'Hand crafts are interesting'). A thesis that merely says the issue is complicated, with no claim about what should be done, earns 0.
Evidence and Commentary (0-4): Strong evidence for this task is concrete: a particular object made or botched, a specific skill the writer or someone they observed could not learn from a screen, a described workplace where manual judgment still mattered, or a reasoned account of what ninety hours of statistics or coding would actually buy a particular student. Invented statistics or appeals to unnamed 'studies' should be treated as general assertion, not specific evidence. Commentary should connect evidence to the requirement question, not merely praise or dismiss craft in the abstract.
   - 4: Provides specific, well-chosen evidence and consistently explains how it supports the claim, so that the essay develops a line of reasoning rather than a list. The essay engages the real tension in the prompt (opportunity cost versus what a person loses by never making anything) and does something with it: concedes, limits, or refutes. Evidence may come from personal experience, observation, or reading as long as it is concrete and the commentary makes its relevance explicit.
   - 3: Provides specific evidence and the commentary explains how each piece supports the thesis. The line of reasoning is clear and mostly consistent, but at least one step is underdeveloped, or the essay handles the strongest objection (the ninety-hours-is-ninety-hours tradeoff) only by naming it rather than answering it.
   - 2: Provides some specific evidence (a remembered shop class, a grandparent who sewed, an observation about a repair shop, something read about apprenticeship or about automated manufacturing), but the commentary explains the evidence only loosely or the examples do not build toward a single line of reasoning. Typical of this level: a list of three unrelated examples each followed by one sentence of explanation.
   - 1: Evidence is mostly general assertion ('everyone knows working with your hands builds character') or a summary of the Pellingham dispute with no new material. Commentary, if present, repeats the evidence rather than explaining it.
   - 0: Only restates the thesis, repeats the stimulus, or offers evidence unconnected to any claim.
Sophistication (0-1): Earned sophistication for this task usually comes from questioning an assumption shared by both sides in the stimulus: that time in school is a fixed quantity to be allocated efficiently, or that usefulness is the right measure. Reframing the wobbling chair as the point of the class restates the board chair's own position and is not sophistication by itself. Simply mentioning both sides is not sophistication; doing something with the tension is.
   - 1: The essay does at least one of the following in a sustained way: explores a tension inside its own position (for example, that the value of a craft may depend on its being chosen, which a requirement undermines); situates the question in a wider context (what schools are for, who gets to decide what students will 'actually need', how prediction about future work has failed before); draws a distinction the stimulus does not make (between craft as job training and craft as a way of meeting consequences); or writes with a controlled, specific voice that advances the argument rather than decorating it.
   - 0: The argument stays at the level of the stimulus, treats the question as a simple yes or no, uses a mechanical five-paragraph structure with generic transitions, or attempts complexity only through an unsupported gesture ('on the other hand, some people disagree'). Ornate language without added thought does not earn the point.
Note: Score the thesis row first and independently; an essay can earn the thesis point and still score low on evidence.
Note: A qualified position is not automatically more sophisticated than an unqualified one. Judge sophistication by what the essay does with its position, not by hedging.
Note: Personal experience is fully acceptable evidence; weigh it by its specificity and by how well the commentary links it to the requirement question.
Note: Do not reward essays for quoting the stimulus at length. The stimulus is a prompt, not a source to be analyzed.
Note: An essay that argues against the requirement is scored on exactly the same terms as one that argues for it.
Note: Length is not a criterion. A short essay with a tight line of reasoning can earn a 4 on row B.

Sample response, high score (6/6; Thesis 1, Evidence and commentary 4, Sophistication 1):
In eighth grade I glued up a maple cutting board with the grain running the wrong way, and three weeks later it split down the middle on my mom's counter. Nobody had to grade it. The board graded itself. I thought about that board while reading about the parents in Pellingham, because they are right that a machine could have made a better one in a minute. But they are missing what the crack taught me. Schools should require a hand craft, but only if it is taught as practice in living with mistakes that cannot be undone, not as a weak copy of factory training, and only if students get to choose the craft and the requirement is shorter than a full year.

The parents' best argument is about time, and it deserves a real answer. My friend Marcus wants to study computer science, and ninety more hours of coding would probably get him one more finished project for his portfolio. That matters. But the thing that makes coding easy to practice is also what limits it as a teacher. When Marcus breaks his program he hits Ctrl-Z or goes back to an earlier version, and the mistake disappears like it never happened. When I made my second board I measured three times before every cut, not because Mr. Halloran told me to, but because I had already watched one split. Coding and statistics teach students to be correct eventually. They are worse at teaching students to be careful beforehand, because they forgive too easily. A craft class gives Marcus something his other ninety hours can't.

It is also not true that manual judgment has vanished just because machines exist. The mechanic at the bike shop near my house trues wheels by spinning them and plucking the spokes like guitar strings, listening for the one that sounds flat. The shop owns a truing stand that measures automatically, but he told me it "doesn't know when the rim itself is bent." What he has isn't really speed or precision, since the machine beats him at both. What he has is the habit of noticing. That is why I think the parents are measuring the wrong thing when they talk about the chair. They treat the wobbling chair as a failure because a factory chair is better. But a factory chair can't tell you anything about the person who made it, and a wobbling chair is a record of exactly where the student's attention slipped. The point of the class is the wobble.

The parents also assume that school time is a fixed budget that should be spent on what students will "actually need." The problem is that nobody is very good at predicting that. My grandmother's high school required shorthand because every office supposedly needed it, and twenty years later the skill was useless. Some of the coding languages being pushed today may be written mostly by AI before current juniors finish college. If schools can't guess which skills will last, it makes more sense to spend some time on habits that carry over, like patience and taking responsibility for your own mistakes, than to spend every hour betting on the job market.

Still, there is a tension inside my own position. Part of why my cutting board meant something is that I wanted it to turn out well. A student forced into weaving who doesn't care will just put in the hours, and a box-checking requirement could kill the exact attention it is supposed to build. That is why the conditions matter. Students should pick their own craft, the class should be one semester, and grading should reward the reflection on what went wrong, not a polished final product. Pellingham's board chair said the requirement "is not about chairs." She's right, but the school has to actually teach it that way, or the parents will be right too.
   - "Schools should require a hand craft, but only if it is taught as practice in living with mistakes that cannot be undone" - This is a defensible, qualified thesis that takes a side on the requirement itself. It also sets the conditions the essay will argue for later: craft taught as meeting consequences, student choice, a shorter term. Someone could reasonably disagree with it, so it earns the point.
   - "only if students get to choose the craft and the requirement is shorter than a full year" - These conditions set up the line of reasoning and come back in the conclusion, so the thesis organizes the whole essay instead of sitting in one sentence.
   - "The board graded itself." - The opening uses a specific botched object as evidence, which the rubric names as strong evidence for this task. The essay returns to it later as proof of a change in behavior.
   - "ninety more hours of coding would probably get him one more finished project for his portfolio" - This takes on the strongest objection, the ninety-hours tradeoff, with a concrete account of what those hours would buy one particular student. It answers the objection rather than just naming it, which is what a 4 requires.
   - "They are worse at teaching students to be careful beforehand, because they forgive too easily." - This is commentary, not summary. It explains why the cutting-board evidence answers the opportunity-cost objection by contrasting mistakes you can undo with mistakes you can't.
   - "listening for the one that sounds flat" - This is an observed workplace where manual judgment still matters. The commentary that follows ties it to the reasoning (craft as a habit of noticing, not speed), so it builds the argument instead of adding a separate example to a list.
   - "My grandmother's high school required shorthand" - This is concrete evidence that predictions about future work have failed before. It directly challenges the parents' claim about what students will 'actually need.'
   - "The point of the class is the wobble." - The essay answers the parents' assumption that the wobbling chair is a failure by reframing the flaw as the purpose of the class, and it adds its own reason: the wobble records where attention slipped. The preceding paragraph builds to this, so the move is sustained.
   - "The parents also assume that school time is a fixed budget" - This places the debate in a wider context: what schools are for, and whether anyone can predict which skills students will need. It goes past the yes-or-no framing of the stimulus.
   - "there is a tension inside my own position" - The essay explores a tension inside its own position: forcing a craft may undermine the attention that gives it value. It then uses that tension to justify the conditions in the thesis rather than just pointing it out. This supports the sophistication point.

Sample response, middle score (4/6; Thesis 1, Evidence and commentary 3, Sophistication 0):
I think schools should require a hand craft, but only for a limited amount of time and only if it is taught as a way of solving problems and not as job training. A full year of ninety hours for everybody is probably too much, but a semester that counts toward electives the students already have would be worth it.

The main reason is that making something by hand teaches you to deal with mistakes. In eighth grade I took a shop class where we had to build a small wooden toolbox. I measured one side wrong and cut it too short, and there was no undo button. I had to either start over with new wood or figure out a way to fix it, and I ended up adding a strip of wood to the bottom that made the box look kind of strange. The box was not good, but I remember what I learned from it. When you cannot delete a mistake you have to think about it before you do it. That is the same thing the board's chair meant when she said the requirement is not about chairs. A student who learns that carefulness in a shop might use it later when writing a paper or doing a lab, even if she never touches a saw again.

The parents have a point, though, that ninety hours is ninety hours. A student who wants to be an engineer might get more out of coding or statistics. But I think this objection assumes that school time is only for things that will be directly useful later. My uncle works as a mechanic and he says that the computers in cars can tell you what is wrong, but you still need to know how it feels when a bolt is about to strip. That shows that even in a world of machines some jobs still need hands. Also, nobody really knows which skills students will actually need, so a school that only teaches what looks useful now could be making a bad guess.

For this reason I would not make the requirement a full year. Machines really do make better chairs, so the point should not be the finished product. If the class is a semester and the students can pick which craft they do, then the cost is smaller and the benefit is still there. Students who choose bicycle repair or weaving will care more about it than students who are just forced into woodworking.

In conclusion, schools should require a short hand craft course because it teaches students to live with their mistakes, but they should keep it limited so it does not take too much time from other subjects.
   - "I think schools should require a hand craft, but only for a limited amount of time and only if it is taught as a way of solving problems and not as job training." - Defensible, qualified thesis that commits to a stance on how far and under what conditions the requirement is worthwhile, so it earns the thesis point.
   - "I measured one side wrong and cut it too short, and there was no undo button." - Specific personal example (the toolbox) that is concrete and tied to the requirement question, which is the essay's strongest evidence.
   - "A student who learns that carefulness in a shop might use it later when writing a paper or doing a lab, even if she never touches a saw again." - Commentary links the example to the claim, but the transfer to other tasks is asserted rather than shown, so the reasoning is underdeveloped.
   - "But I think this objection assumes that school time is only for things that will be directly useful later." - Engages the ninety-hours tradeoff and starts to question the usefulness assumption, but the answer is brief and does not weigh what coding or statistics would actually buy a student.
   - "My uncle works as a mechanic and he says that the computers in cars can tell you what is wrong, but you still need to know how it feels when a bolt is about to strip." - Specific observation about manual judgment in a workplace, but it is secondhand and only loosely connected to why all students should be required to take a craft.
   - "nobody really knows which skills students will actually need, so a school that only teaches what looks useful now could be making a bad guess." - Gestures at the unreliability of predicting future needs, a possible sophisticated move, but it is a single unsupported sentence and not sustained.
   - "Students who choose bicycle repair or weaving will care more about it than students who are just forced into woodworking." - Hints at a tension between choice and requirement but does not explore it, and the conclusion largely restates the thesis, so sophistication is not earned.

Sample response, low score (1/6; Thesis 0, Evidence and commentary 1, Sophistication 0):
In Pellingham the school board wants every student to learn a hand craft before they graduate and some parents do not like it. I think there are good points on both sides of this issue and schools should think about it carefully.

On one hand, learning a craft is good for students. Working with your hands teaches you things that you cant learn from a book or a screen. Everyone knows that making something builds character and makes people more patient. The board chair said it is not about chairs and I agree with that. Even if a machine can make a better chair, a student who makes one will feel proud of it.

On the other hand, ninety hours is a lot of time. Students need to be ready for the future and the future is technology. Coding and statistics are things that jobs will need, so some parents are right to be worried. Machines do most of the work now anyway so a lot of people will never need to cut wood or sew.

In my own experience I took a shop class in ninth grade and we made a small birdhouse. Mine was not very good but I still liked it. It was fun to do something different from regular classes.

In conclusion, hand crafts can be valuable but so can other subjects. Schools should decide what is best for their students and balance the two things. There are many opinions about this topic but in the end education is about learning and both skills matter.
   - "I think there are good points on both sides of this issue and schools should think about it carefully." - No defensible position on the requirement. This only says the issue has two sides and should be considered carefully, which earns no thesis credit.
   - "Schools should decide what is best for their students and balance the two things." - The conclusion repeats the non-committal stance. It never says how far a craft requirement should go or under what conditions, so a reader has nothing to disagree with.
   - "Everyone knows that making something builds character and makes people more patient." - General assertion with no concrete example. The claim is praise of craft in the abstract and is not tied to the requirement question.
   - "I took a shop class in ninth grade and we made a small birdhouse." - This is the only specific evidence, but the commentary stops at 'it was fun.' It never explains what the birdhouse shows about whether every student should be required to do this.
   - "Coding and statistics are things that jobs will need, so some parents are right to be worried." - The ninety-hours objection is named and mostly repeats the stimulus. The essay does not weigh what those hours would buy against what craft offers, so the central tension goes unanswered.
   - "There are many opinions about this topic but in the end education is about learning and both skills matter." - This is a generic gesture at both sides within a mechanical intro, body and conclusion structure. It questions no assumption, such as time being a fixed quantity or usefulness being the measure, so there is no sophistication.

   - "A student who learns that carefulness in a shop might use it later when writing a paper or doing a lab, even if she never touches a saw again." - Commentary links the example to the claim, but the transfer to other tasks is asserted rather than shown, so the reasoning is underdeveloped.
   - "But I think this objection assumes that school time is only for things that will be directly useful later." - Engages the ninety-hours tradeoff and starts to question the usefulness assumption, but the answer is brief and does not weigh what coding or statistics would actually buy a student.
   - "My uncle works as a mechanic and he says that the computers in cars can tell you what is wrong, but you still need to know how it feels when a bolt is about to strip." - Specific observation about manual judgment in a workplace, but it is secondhand and only loosely connected to why all students should be required to take a craft.
   - "nobody really knows which skills students will actually need, so a school that only teaches what looks useful now could be making a bad guess." - Gestures at the unreliability of predicting future needs, a possible sophisticated move, but it is a single unsupported sentence and not sustained.
   - "Students who choose bicycle repair or weaving will care more about it than students who are just forced into woodworking." - Hints at a tension between choice and requirement but does not explore it, and the conclusion largely restates the thesis, so sophistication is not earned.

Sample response, low score (1/6; Thesis 0, Evidence and commentary 1, Sophistication 0):
In Pellingham the school board wants every student to learn a hand craft before they graduate and some parents do not like it. I think there are good points on both sides of this issue and schools should think about it carefully.

On one hand, learning a craft is good for students. Working with your hands teaches you things that you cant learn from a book or a screen. Everyone knows that making something builds character and makes people more patient. The board chair said it is not about chairs and I agree with that. Even if a machine can make a better chair, a student who makes one will feel proud of it.

On the other hand, ninety hours is a lot of time. Students need to be ready for the future and the future is technology. Coding and statistics are things that jobs will need, so some parents are right to be worried. Machines do most of the work now anyway so a lot of people will never need to cut wood or sew.

In my own experience I took a shop class in ninth grade and we made a small birdhouse. Mine was not very good but I still liked it. It was fun to do something different from regular classes.

In conclusion, hand crafts can be valuable but so can other subjects. Schools should decide what is best for their students and balance the two things. There are many opinions about this topic but in the end education is about learning and both skills matter.
   - "I think there are good points on both sides of this issue and schools should think about it carefully." - No defensible position on the requirement. This only says the issue has two sides and should be considered carefully, which earns no thesis credit.
   - "Schools should decide what is best for their students and balance the two things." - The conclusion repeats the non-committal stance. It never says how far a craft requirement should go or under what conditions, so a reader has nothing to disagree with.
   - "Everyone knows that making something builds character and makes people more patient." - General assertion with no concrete example. The claim is praise of craft in the abstract and is not tied to the requirement question.
   - "I took a shop class in ninth grade and we made a small birdhouse." - This is the only specific evidence, but the commentary stops at 'it was fun.' It never explains what the birdhouse shows about whether every student should be required to do this.
   - "Coding and statistics are things that jobs will need, so some parents are right to be worried." - The ninety-hours objection is named and mostly repeats the stimulus. The essay does not weigh what those hours would buy against what craft offers, so the central tension goes unanswered.
   - "There are many opinions about this topic but in the end education is about learning and both skills matter." - This is a generic gesture at both sides within a mechanical intro, body and conclusion structure. It questions no assumption, such as time being a fixed quantity or usefulness being the measure, so there is no sophistication.

The Chair That Wobbles
Odalys Vreeland, column in the Kettle Hill Quarterly (fictional), 2026

When the school board in Pellingham voted last spring to require every student to complete a year of a hand craft before graduating (woodworking, weaving, bookbinding, bicycle repair, whatever the shop could staff), the objections came fast. Parents asked why a teenager who will never cut a dovetail joint should spend ninety hours learning to. A machine in a factory two states away can produce a flawless chair in minutes; the student's chair will wobble. But the board's chair answered with a question of her own: what does a person lose who has never made anything with her hands, never felt a plane bite too deep, never had to live with a mistake she cannot undo by pressing a key? One of them pointed out that ninety hours is ninety hours not spent on statistics, or coding, or the languages the students will actually need.

ALTON original passage
Eight Bars at the Grange Hall

[1] Last Thursday I sat in the back row of the Fenwick Grange Hall while the Marrow Creek Community Orchestra rehearsed for its spring concert. [2] Orchestras are interesting and say a lot about people. [3] Forty-one players showed up, from a fourteen-year-old violist to a retired mail carrier who has played second trombone for thirty years.

[4] Conductor Abel Ostrander stopped the group six times in the first piece, each time over the same eight bars. [5] The flutes were rushing, the cellos were dragging, and nobody could hear the oboe. [6] Ostrander did not single anyone out; instead, he asked every section except the oboe to play the passage half as loud. [7] By the fourth try, the oboe melody floated clearly over the whole ensemble. [8] Every musician in an orchestra always cares more about the group than about his or her own part.

[9] During the break, the cellists told me their section meets on Sunday afternoons to work through tricky passages together. [10] Players share music stands, and the woodwinds carry spare reeds for anyone who forgets theirs. [11] The orchestra holds no auditions, anyone who can read music is welcome. [12] Our town council, which spent last winter arguing over a parking lot could learn something from them.

[13] Anyway, that is what I saw at the rehearsal.

pub.passage:
ALTON original passage
Standing on Her Work

¶1 One Tuesday last October, a date-formatting library called tidyclock vanished from the public package registry, and by morning several thousand websites could no longer tell their users what day it was. Its sole maintainer, a retired schoolteacher in Pell Harbor, had deleted it after a decade of unpaid work and one rude bug report too many. Desmond Alcock's new book, Nobody's Job, opens with that night, and it is the right place to begin. I spent nine years maintaining a small text-parsing library used by companies I was never allowed to name, so I read Alcock with the uneasy attention of a patient reading her own chart.

¶2 The book's first half is a diagnosis, and it is a good one. Alcock surveyed four hundred of the most heavily downloaded packages in three programming languages and found that more than half depended on a single active volunteer. He calls these projects load-bearing walls that no inspector has visited, and the metaphor earns its keep: the walls are hidden inside the plaster of every bank, hospital, and school district that runs code on top of them. Nobody chose this arrangement. It accreted, one convenient download at a time, until the whole structure rested on the patience of people who could stop at any moment and owed us nothing if they did.

¶3 It is in the second half, where Alcock turns from diagnosis to cure, that the book loses its footing. His remedy is sponsorship: corporations that profit from open-source software should fund its maintainers, and he describes several foundations that already do so. I will grant that money has saved projects. A stipend kept at least one widely used encryption library alive after its maintainer nearly quit, and Alcock tells that story well. But a stipend changes what the work is. Consider the neighbor who shovels the shared walkway every winter because no one else will; the day you start paying her, the shoveling becomes a service, the snow becomes her problem, and you acquire the right to complain about ice. Sponsorship converts a gift into a contract, and the contract arrives written in the sponsor's priorities, not the project's.

¶4 I know something about how such gifts are received. In nine years I received roughly four thousand bug reports, most of them phrased as demands, several of them threatening, and one, from a hospital network in a city I have never visited, that began with the words "thank you." One. Did any of those four thousand correspondents imagine that a person, rather than a department, was reading them at eleven at night? Alcock understands this loneliness better than any writer I have read, which is precisely why his faith in a check is so puzzling.

¶5 The better cure is already visible in the margins of his own book, though he never names it. The institutions that depend on these libraries do not lack money; they lack a sense that the maintenance is theirs to do. A regional bank runs tidyclock on its login page, employs ninety engineers, and has never assigned one of them a Friday afternoon to review tidyclock's open issues. Volunteer fire departments survive not because the town mails a check to the one person who owns a hose but because the people whose houses would burn show up for the drills. The obligation should attach to dependence, not to profit, and it should be paid in hours, not dollars. This will not rescue every project, and the smallest libraries will still rely on the stubbornness of individuals; but it would spread the weight across the walls that bear it.

¶6 Nobody's Job deserves the wide readership it will probably get. Read it for the first half, which will frighten you in the right way, and argue with the second, which will comfort you in the wrong one. The retired schoolteacher in Pell Harbor did not need a sponsor. She needed the several thousand of us who were standing on her work to notice that we were.

pub.passage:
ALTON original passage
Who Wrote the English Sentences

¶1 Last Tuesday the Ambervale Prize announced its shortlist, and the press release named six novels, six authors, and six publishers, but not one translator. Four of those six books were written in languages the jury does not read. I know this because I translated one of them. My name appears on page four of the paperback, in a typeface smaller than the one used to describe the paper stock.

¶2 Readers sometimes imagine translation as a kind of plumbing: the words flow in one end of the pipe in Norwegian and come out the other end in English, and the translator merely checks for leaks. The image is comforting, and it is wrong. A sentence in one language is not a container with a fixed amount of meaning inside it; it is a set of choices that a second language cannot reproduce but can only answer. When the Norwegian novelist Sigrun Aalvik wrote that her heroine "went out into the weather," she used a verb that in her dialect also means to quarrel. English has no such verb. I had to decide whether the woman walked into a storm or into an argument, and whichever I chose, the English reader would believe the author had chosen it.

¶3 Consider the scale of the problem. Aalvik's novel runs to roughly ninety thousand words, and I made, by my own rough count, something near forty decisions a page that no dictionary could make for me: where to break a sentence, which of three possible synonyms carried the right chill, whether a joke survived or had to be replaced with a different joke. Multiply that by three hundred pages and you arrive at an English book that shares a plot and a spirit with the Norwegian one but shares none of its sentences. Every sentence the English reader admires, I wrote. Every sentence the reader finds clumsy, I also wrote.

¶4 I can hear the objection, because I have made it myself at dinner parties: the story, the characters, the architecture of the book belong to Aalvik, and the translator is at most a skilled carpenter working from her drawings. There is something to this. I did not invent the heroine, and I would not want credit for her. But a carpenter who selects every board, every joint, and every finish, and whose work the client lives inside for years, is not usually left off the plaque. Architecture is credited; so is the building.

¶5 Why, then, does the convention of the invisible translator persist? Partly because publishers fear that a second name on the cover warns the buyer that the book is foreign, and foreign, in the sales meeting, means difficult. Partly because reviewers, who seldom read the original, find it easier to praise "the author's luminous prose" than to admit they are praising prose whose author they cannot identify. And partly, I confess, because translators themselves have cultivated a monkish modesty, as though visibility were a kind of vanity. The effect is circular: because we are unnamed, we seem unimportant, and because we seem unimportant, nobody thinks to name us.

¶6 I am not asking for the author's name to be removed, or shrunk, or shared with mine in some awkward hyphenated compound. I am asking for a line of type on the front of the book, the same size as the blurb from a novelist nobody has heard of, that says who wrote the English sentences. If you run a prize, name the translator in the press release. If you review books, say which words you are actually quoting. And if you are a reader who has ever loved a novel written in a language you do not speak, you have already loved a translator's work; you simply were not told whom to thank.

pub.passage:
ALTON original passage
Who Wrote the English Sentences

¶1 Last Tuesday the Ambervale Prize announced its shortlist, and the press release named six novels, six authors, and six publishers, but not one translator. Four of those six books were written in languages the jury does not read. I know this because I translated one of them. My name appears on page four of the paperback, in a typeface smaller than the one used to describe the paper stock.

¶2 Readers sometimes imagine translation as a kind of plumbing: the words flow in one end of the pipe in Norwegian and come out the other end in English, and the translator merely checks for leaks. The image is comforting, and it is wrong. A sentence in one language is not a container with a fixed amount of meaning inside it; it is a set of choices that a second language cannot reproduce but can only answer. When the Norwegian novelist Sigrun Aalvik wrote that her heroine "went out into the weather," she used a verb that in her dialect also means to quarrel. English has no such verb. I had to decide whether the woman walked into a storm or into an argument, and whichever I chose, the English reader would believe the author had chosen it.

¶3 Consider the scale of the problem. Aalvik's novel runs to roughly ninety thousand words, and I made, by my own rough count, something near forty decisions a page that no dictionary could make for me: where to break a sentence, which of three possible synonyms carried the right chill, whether a joke survived or had to be replaced with a different joke. Multiply that by three hundred pages and you arrive at an English book that shares a plot and a spirit with the Norwegian one but shares none of its sentences. Every sentence the English reader admires, I wrote. Every sentence the reader finds clumsy, I also wrote.

¶4 I can hear the objection, because I have made it myself at dinner parties: the story, the characters, the architecture of the book belong to Aalvik, and the translator is at most a skilled carpenter working from her drawings. There is something to this. I did not invent the heroine, and I would not want credit for her. But a carpenter who selects every board, every joint, and every finish, and whose work the client lives inside for years, is not usually left off the plaque. Architecture is credited; so is the building.

¶5 Why, then, does the convention of the invisible translator persist? Partly because publishers fear that a second name on the cover warns the buyer that the book is foreign, and foreign, in the sales meeting, means difficult. Partly because reviewers, who seldom read the original, find it easier to praise "the author's luminous prose" than to admit they are praising prose whose author they cannot identify. And partly, I confess, because translators themselves have cultivated a monkish modesty, as though visibility were a kind of vanity. The effect is circular: because we are unnamed, we seem unimportant, and because we seem unimportant, nobody thinks to name us.

¶6 I am not asking for the author's name to be removed, or shrunk, or shared with mine in some awkward hyphenated compound. I am asking for a line of type on the front of the book, the same size as the blurb from a novelist nobody has heard of, that says who wrote the English sentences. If you run a prize, name the translator in the press release. If you review books, say which words you are actually quoting. And if you are a reader who has ever loved a novel written in a language you do not speak, you have already loved a translator's work; you simply were not told whom to thank.

Let Cutler's Marsh Flood Again

[1] Behind the Brambleton subdivision, past the last cul-de-sac, lies a flat field of cattails and cracked drainage pipe that most of us have never noticed. [2] Forty years ago it was Cutler's Marsh, until a developer dug ditches to dry it out for houses that were never built. [3] Wetlands are important for many reasons.

[4] This spring the Larkfield town council will vote on whether to spend 180,000 dollars to fill those ditches and let the marsh hold water again. [5] Restoring the marsh would definitely end flooding in Brambleton forever. [6] Last April, after two days of rain, water reached the doorsteps on Finch Lane, and the town paid 64,000 dollars to pump out basements. [7] A marsh works like a sponge, soaking up runoff and releasing it slowly.

[8] Some residents totally freak out about mosquitoes. [9] An ecologist hired by the town, Ilse Varga, reported that a healthy marsh draws dragonflies and frogs that eat mosquito larvae.

[10] Our biology classes could use the marsh as an outdoor lab, measuring water quality instead of just reading about it. [11] Anyway, the council should totally go for it, because it's a no-brainer.

pub.passage:
ALTON original passage
Sixty-One Sycamores

¶1 When I was twenty-three and newly hired by the town of Harrow Fen, my supervisor handed me a clipboard and told me to count the trees on Calder Avenue. I assumed it was busywork. It took four days, because every sycamore on that street had something to say: a hollow where a raccoon had raised three litters, a lightning scar healed over like a closed eye, a root that had lifted a sidewalk slab and then, with a patience I did not yet understand, grown around it. Graduates, I have been asked to speak to you about your futures, and I intend to, but I am going to do it by talking about those sycamores, because last Tuesday the council voted to widen Calder Avenue, and the plan calls for removing all sixty-one of them.

¶2 Let me be precise about what we mean when we say old-growth on a city street, since the phrase was borrowed from forestry and does not fit perfectly. In a forest, old growth describes a stand that has never been cleared. On a street, it describes something rarer: a tree that has survived a century of paving, trenching, salt, and committees. Every one of those sycamores was planted by a person who knew they would never sit in its shade. That is not sentiment; that is the definition.

¶3 You have spent years learning to call things by their proper names, so call a street tree what it is: infrastructure. A storm sewer carries water away; a mature sycamore intercepts roughly three thousand gallons of rainfall a year before it ever reaches the sewer. A transformer cools a block in August; the canopy on Calder lowers surface temperature by double digits, according to the thermal survey our own department commissioned seven years ago. We do not demolish a bridge because it is old. We inspect it, we repair it, and when we must, we close a lane. Yet the same council that budgets forty years of maintenance for a culvert will vote to erase a hundred and forty years of canopy in an afternoon, because a tree, unlike a culvert, does not appear on the balance sheet as an asset that depreciates.

¶4 I will concede the obvious. Some old trees must come down. I have signed the removal orders myself, standing under a red oak with a fungal rot that had eaten two-thirds of its heartwood, and I did not sleep well afterward, but I signed. A dangerous tree is not a monument; it is a liability with leaves. But the Calder sycamores are not dangerous. The widening is proposed so that traffic can move eleven seconds faster at the Pell Street light. Eleven seconds. We are being asked to trade a century for a fraction of a minute, and to call the trade progress.

¶5 So here is what I am asking of you, and it is harder than it sounds. You will be the ones in the room when the next Calder Avenue comes up for a vote. You will have the drawings, the models, the cost estimates, and you will be tempted to treat a mature tree the way the software treats it: as a circle on a plan, easily erased and easily redrawn somewhere else. Resist that. A sapling planted in mitigation is not a replacement; it is an IOU that will not be paid during your career, or your children's. Insist that the removal of an old-growth street tree be justified the way we justify closing a hospital wing: reluctantly, publicly, and with the arithmetic on the table.

¶6 I counted sixty-one sycamores in my first week of work. I would like to count them again at the end of yours. Go and be the kind of planners who make that possible.

pub.passage:
ALTON original passage
The Hand That Drew It: Remembering Teodora Quist

¶1 Teodora Quist kept a jar of eraser crumbs on her drafting table and told every new apprentice that it was the most honest record of her career. She died last month in Lower Marrow at eighty-one, in the house behind the county survey office where she had drawn maps for forty-three years. She taught a generation of us that a map is not a picture of the world. It is a case made about the world, built with the same tools as any other case: selection, emphasis, and omission.

¶2 Most people would say a map is a drawing that shows where things are. Quist would say it is a drawing that shows which things the mapmaker decided you should know are there. A sheet of paper cannot hold a county; it holds perhaps a thousandth of what a county contains, and the rest must be left off. Every blank space, she liked to say, is a verdict. The road drawn thick and the stream drawn thin, the village named and the settlement unnamed, the boundary inked solid and the boundary left dotted: these are not observations but rulings.

¶3 The clearest demonstration came when the Marrow County Board asked her office for a map to accompany a vote on building along the river's lower terrace. Standard practice would have been to shade the floodplain in the pale blue the state style guide recommended, a blue so gentle it reads as decoration. Quist shaded it in a mud brown no one could mistake for ornament, and she printed the crest of the 1961 flood at every bridge. The developers' attorney called the map inflammatory. She answered that the pale blue was also inflammatory; it simply inflamed in the other direction. The board voted nine to two against the project, and three members later said the brown was what they remembered when they voted.

¶4 Her critics, and she had them, said this proved she was an advocate who happened to own a drafting pen rather than a surveyor who happened to have opinions. I will grant them half of that. She did want the project stopped, and she said so to anyone who asked. But the charge assumes that somewhere a map exists with no advocate behind it, a sheet that merely reports, and in forty-three years she never saw one and neither have I. The pale blue floodplain had an advocate too; he was just quieter about it. What distinguished Quist was not that her maps argued but that she signed the argument.

¶5 She trained apprentices with a single exercise, repeated until it became reflex. Given one set of survey data for a single square mile, we drew three maps: one for a family thinking of buying a house there, one for a company planning a pipeline, and one for a child who would walk to school along its lanes. The data never changed. The maps never matched. The buyer's map grew contour lines and drainage; the pipeline's map grew easements and bedrock; the child's map grew crossings, dogs, and the one hedge you could cut through. After the third round, nobody could say "just the facts" with a straight face, which was, I think, the whole point.

¶6 The week after she died I went to the survey office, mostly to sit in the chair, and the jar of eraser crumbs was still there, fuller than I remembered. It struck me that she had kept it because it was, in its way, her finest map: a record of every line she had chosen, on reflection, not to let stand. We will mourn her, and we will do it properly. But I would ask anyone reading this, the next time a map is unfolded at a council meeting or on a phone screen, to do what she did and look first for the hand that drew it. Ask what it was told to show you. Then ask what it was told to leave out.

pub.explanation:
Scoring guide (ALTON practice rubric, not official College Board scoring). Each essay is worth 6 points.
Thesis (0-1): Acceptable theses identify at least one specific choice or pattern (the kitchen metaphor, the concession in paragraph 3, the Anna Belle anecdote, the shift from economic to moral framing, the piloting metaphor that frames the whole speech) and link it to the goal of defeating the rezoning. A thesis that lists devices with no claim about effect ('Osgood uses metaphor, statistics, and a story') is on the line; award the point only if the essay's thesis, wherever it appears, attaches those devices to a specific purpose; a generic purpose ('to persuade the town') does not count.
   - 1: A defensible claim about how Osgood's choices work toward her purpose. The claim may be modest (for example, that she establishes herself as a practical insider and then redefines the wharf as infrastructure rather than a business) but it must name a rhetorical move or strategy and connect it to persuading the town to keep the wharf working. The thesis may appear anywhere in the essay and may be more than one sentence.
   - 0: No thesis, or a thesis that only restates the prompt (for example, 'Osgood uses many rhetorical choices to persuade the town'), or a statement that merely summarizes what Osgood says about the wharf without making a claim about how she persuades. A thesis that takes a position on whether the wharf should be rezoned, rather than on Osgood's rhetoric, also earns 0.
Evidence and Commentary (0-4): Choices that count as valid evidence include: the opening ethos and antithesis (sentences 1-4); the description of the brochure and the pointed absence (8-9); the concession and rebuttal (10-15); the kitchen metaphor and restaurant analogy (14-16); the enumeration of trades and the direct address 'half of you' (17); the cause-and-effect chain with 'Then' repetition and the two clipped sentences (19-20) before the longer sentence about the kids (21); the statistics and their scaling to a town of six thousand (22-23); the tone shift and anecdote (24-30), including the short sentences 'It cannot. Nobody is aboard.'; the rhetorical question and redefinition of the decision (31-33); the personification 'it answers back' and the parallel verbs (35-36); the closing metaphor of bringing a town in (38-39) and the conciliatory offer about the culvert (41). Essays need not use these labels; what matters is accurate description of the move and explanation of its effect. Merely noting that Osgood 'uses numbers' is weak; noting that she volunteers the unflattering numbers first (12) so the favorable ones (22) land as honest counts for more.
   - 4: Specific, well-chosen evidence from across the passage supports a sustained line of reasoning. Commentary consistently explains how choices function for this audience: for example, why the concession about the ice house and fuel dock makes the later kitchen metaphor credible, why the Anna Belle story is placed after the numbers rather than before, or how the closing piloting metaphor returns to the ethos of the opening. The essay shows how choices work together rather than as a checklist.
   - 3: Specific evidence from several parts of the passage, with commentary that explains how at least two or three choices serve the purpose in ways tied to this audience and occasion. The essay has a line of reasoning, but one or more body paragraphs may slip into summary, or the analysis may be uneven (strong on the anecdote, generic on the opening ethos).
   - 2: Quotes or closely references specific moments and names the choices accurately, but commentary is thin or repetitive: it asserts that a choice 'makes the audience feel' or 'helps her argument' without explaining the mechanism. Typical 2 essays treat each device in isolation and do not connect them to the exigence (an imminent council vote on a developer's proposal).
   - 1: Mostly summary or paraphrase of Osgood's points about the wharf with little attention to how she says them. Evidence, if quoted, is general and commentary consists of labels ('this is pathos') with no explanation of effect on the town-meeting audience.
   - 0: Restates the thesis, summarizes the speech, or offers evidence that is not from the passage.
Sophistication (0-1): A strong candidate for this point notices that Osgood never attacks the developers, that she borrows the brochure's own silence (no forklifts) as her strongest exhibit, or that the Anna Belle story quietly reframes the question from money to safety and who is physically present on the water. Do not award the point for simply using the word 'juxtaposition' or for an eloquent conclusion attached to an otherwise formulaic essay.
   - 1: The essay does one or more of the following convincingly and throughout rather than in a single sentence: explains how the structure of the speech works as a whole (the movement from credibility, to concession, to economics, to the rescue story, to redefinition, to the closing ask); examines tensions in Osgood's rhetoric, such as the risk that a retired pilot's nostalgia could read as self-interest and how she heads that off by conceding the fleet's decline and ending with an offer to solve the culvert problem; situates the speech in its rhetorical situation by considering what council members and residents who favor the tax revenue would need to hear; or writes with a consistently precise and controlled prose style.
   - 0: Competent analysis that stays at the level of device plus effect, or an essay whose attempts at complexity are decorative (ornate vocabulary, sweeping claims about 'society') rather than analytical.
Note: Score holistically within each row; an essay that earns 4 in Row B will almost always also earn the thesis point, but check that the claim is about rhetoric, not about the merits of rezoning.
Note: Students may describe the choices without technical names. 'She stacks three short sentences so the loss sounds like dominoes falling' is full-credit commentary on sentences 19-21 even without the word 'repetition'.
Note: Essays that argue Osgood is wrong or right about the wharf are off task; score them only on whatever rhetorical analysis they contain.
Note: An essay built on one well-analyzed section (for example, only paragraph 5) can reach a 3 in Row B if the commentary is rich, but reaching 4 requires evidence from more than one part of the speech.
Note: Misreadings that distort the passage (for example, claiming Osgood opposes any change or that she dismisses the town's money problems) cap Row B at 2 because the commentary rests on a false account of the text.

Sample response, high score (6/6; Thesis 1, Evidence and commentary 4, Sophistication 1):
When Marguerite Osgood stood up at the Tillet's Reach town meeting, she was speaking to an audience that already knew the wharf was losing money. The developer's proposal had a simple pitch: handsome condos and cafes, and the tax money that comes with them. Osgood could not win by pretending those numbers away. Instead she builds her speech like one of her channel crossings, carefully and in order. First she earns trust as a practical insider who admits the wharf's weaknesses. Then she redefines the wharf from a failing business into infrastructure the town cannot function without. Finally she shifts the question from money to who is actually on the water when something goes wrong. By the end, a vote that looked like a budget decision feels like a decision about what kind of town Tillet's Reach wants to be.

Osgood opens by shrinking her own authority in a way that actually increases it. "I am not a planner, a developer, or an economist. I am a woman who knows where the rocks are." Listing what she is not lets her step out of the expert argument the council expects, and the plain image of the rocks suggests she knows dangers the planners don't. For an audience of neighbors, someone who climbed "a rope ladder" for thirty-one years is probably more trustworthy than a developer. Then, instead of mocking the brochure, she compliments it: "It is handsome." She never attacks the developers at all. She uses their own drawing as evidence, pointing out that it shows "not a single forklift, fuel barge, or crab pot." The brochure's silence becomes her strongest exhibit, because the audience can see for themselves what the plan leaves out.

The most important move comes in paragraph 3, where Osgood concedes the facts the other side would use against her. The ice house closed, the fuel dock "loses money three months a year," and the town "cannot fix the culvert on Pell Street." By saying these things first, she takes them away from her opponents and shows the council members who want the tax money that she is not just being nostalgic. That concession is what makes the kitchen metaphor work: "It is not a gold mine. It is a kitchen." Nobody judges a kitchen by whether it turns a profit by itself; they judge it by whether the restaurant can run without it. The metaphor changes the standard the wharf is measured by. She then shows the consequences as a chain: "Then the mechanic goes. Then the welder." The sentences get shorter as the town loses more, so the first losses fall like dominoes, and the longer final sentence about the kids who leave carries the damage past the shop floor. And because she already admitted the bad numbers, the good ones, "four million dollars" and "one hundred and forty jobs," sound like honest counts and not a sales pitch.

Osgood saves the Anna Belle story for after the economics, and the placement is deliberate. She even flags the shift, calling it "something now that is harder to put in a brochure." Once the council has heard that the wharf is worth money, she shows that its real value can't be counted. Dale Cuttery reached the trawler in eleven minutes "because they were already there." Then come two blunt sentences: "It cannot. Nobody is aboard." The image of empty shrink-wrapped sailboats quietly turns the debate from profit to safety, and from what the waterfront looks like to who is physically present on it. It is hard to argue for a boardwalk after that without sounding like you'd trade a rescue for a view.

Finally, Osgood returns to where she started. "I have brought a great many ships safely in" sets up her wish "to help bring one town in too." The piloting metaphor ties the ethos of her opening to her request, so she sounds less like an opponent of progress and more like a guide through a dangerous channel. Even her last line, "let us sit down and find another way to pay for the culvert," keeps the concession alive, so nobody in the room has to choose between the wharf and the culvert. Osgood persuades because she never asks the town to ignore its problems. She only asks it to see what the brochure left out.
   - "First she earns trust as a practical insider who admits the wharf's weaknesses. Then she redefines the wharf from a failing business into infrastructure the town cannot function without." - Row A: Defensible, specific thesis that names actual strategies (insider ethos, concession, redefinition as infrastructure, shift to safety) and links them to defeating the rezoning. The First/Then/Finally order also sets up the essay's line of reasoning.
   - "she builds her speech like one of her channel crossings, carefully and in order" - Row C: Sets up the essay's lasting focus on how the whole speech is structured. The body paragraphs follow that sequence, from credibility to concession to economics to the rescue story to the closing ask, so the sophistication point rests on more than one line.
   - "Listing what she is not lets her step out of the expert argument the council expects" - Row B: Explains how the antithesis in sentences 3-4 works on this particular audience instead of just labeling it as ethos.
   - "The brochure's silence becomes her strongest exhibit, because the audience can see for themselves what the plan leaves out." - Row C: Points out that Osgood turns the brochure's own omission into evidence and never attacks the developers. This is one of the insights the rubric names as a sign of sophistication.
   - "That concession is what makes the kitchen metaphor work" - Row B: Shows how two choices work together. The concession in paragraph 3 makes the metaphor believable, so the essay goes beyond treating devices one by one like a checklist.
   - "The sentences get shorter as the town loses more, so the first losses fall like dominoes" - Row B: Describes how sentence length and repetition create an effect in sentences 19-21. This is full-credit commentary even without technical terms.
   - "because she already admitted the bad numbers, the good ones, "four million dollars" and "one hundred and forty jobs," sound like honest counts and not a sales pitch" - Row B: Connects the order of the statistics (unflattering first, favorable later) to credibility. This is exactly the kind of mechanism the rubric rewards.
   - "Osgood saves the Anna Belle story for after the economics, and the placement is deliberate." - Row B: Explains why the story is placed where it is, which the rubric singles out for Row B commentary.
   - "quietly turns the debate from profit to safety, and from what the waterfront looks like to who is physically present on it" - Row C: Recognizes the reframing from money to safety and to who is actually present on the water, which adds complexity to the reading.
   - "keeps the concession alive, so nobody in the room has to choose between the wharf and the culvert" - Row C: Sustains the tension the essay has been tracing, which is how Osgood heads off the charge of nostalgia by taking the town's money problems seriously right through her closing offer.
   - "The piloting metaphor ties the ethos of her opening to her request" - Row B: Links the closing metaphor back to the ethos of the opening, completing a sustained line of reasoning with evidence from across the passage.

Sample response, middle score (4/6; Thesis 1, Evidence and commentary 3, Sophistication 0):
In her speech to the town meeting, Marguerite Osgood tries to convince the council to vote down the rezoning by presenting herself as a practical person who knows the harbor, and then by redefining the north wharf as something the whole town needs instead of just a business that is losing money. She does this through a metaphor, a concession, and a story about a rescue, which together move the audience from thinking about money to thinking about what kind of town they want.

Osgood begins by building her credibility. She says "I am not a planner, a developer, or an economist. I am a woman who knows where the rocks are." By listing what she is not, she sounds humble and not like someone with an agenda, and the line about the rocks makes her sound like she has real experience. This matters because the audience is about to vote on a developer's plan, and she needs them to trust her over a glossy brochure. She also describes the brochure's pictures as having "not a single forklift, fuel barge, or crab pot," which points out what the developer left out and makes the audience notice what would be lost.

   - "Overall, Osgood persuades by being trustworthy, fair, and by making the audience see the wharf differently." - The conclusion repeats the thesis in general terms.
